zh:
【为政第二】

子曰：“为政以德，譬如北辰，居其所而众星共之。”
子曰：“诗三百，一言以蔽之，曰：‘思无邪’。”
子曰：“导之以政，齐之以刑，民免而无耻。导之以德，齐之以礼，有耻且格。”
子曰：“吾十有五而志乎学，三十而立，四十而不惑，五十而知天命，六十而耳顺，七十而纵心所欲，不逾矩。”
孟懿子问孝，子曰：“无违。”樊迟御，子告之曰：“孟孙问孝于我，我对曰：‘无违’。”樊迟曰：“何谓也？”子曰：“生，事之以礼；死，葬之以礼，祭之以礼。”
孟武伯问孝，子曰：“父母唯其疾之忧。”
子游问孝，子曰：“今之孝者，是谓能养。至于犬马，皆能有养。 不敬，何以别乎？”
子夏问孝，子曰：“色难。有事，弟子服其劳，有酒食，先生馔，曾是以为孝乎？”
子曰：“吾与回言终日，不违，如愚。退而省其私，亦足以发，回也不愚。”
子曰：“视其所以，观其所由，察其所安，人焉廋哉？人焉廋哉？”
子曰：“温故而知新，可以为师矣。”
子曰：“君子不器。”
子贡问君子，子曰：“先行其言而后从之。”
子曰：“君子周而不比，小人比而不周。”
子曰：“学而不思则罔，思而不学则殆。”
子曰：“攻乎异端，斯害也已矣。”
子曰：“由，诲汝知之乎？知之为知之，不知为不知，是知也。”
子张学干禄，子曰：“多闻阙疑，慎言其余，则寡尤。多见阙殆，慎行其余，则寡悔。言寡尤，行寡悔，禄在其中矣。”
哀公问曰：“何为则民服？孔子对曰：“举直错诸枉，则民服；举枉错诸直，则民不服。”
季康子问：使民敬、忠以劝，如之何？子曰：“临之以庄，则敬；孝慈，则忠；举善而教不能，则民劝。”
或谓孔子曰：“子奚不为政？子曰：“书云：孝乎惟孝，友于兄弟，施于有政。是亦为政也，奚其为为政也？”
子曰：“人而无信，不知其可也。大车无𫐐，小车无轨，其何以行之哉？”
子张问：“十世可知也？”子曰：“殷因于夏礼，所损益，可知也。周因于殷礼，所损益，可知也。其或继周者，虽百世，亦可知。”
子曰：“非其鬼而祭之，謟也。见义不为，无勇。”
en:
[Chapter 2: Governance]

The Master said, "One who exercises government by means of one's virtue, may be compared to the north polar star, which keeps its place and all the stars turn towards it."
The Master said, "In the Book of Poetry are three hundred pieces, but the design of them all may be embraced in one sentence—'Have no depraved thoughts.'"
The Master said, "If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good."
The Master said, "At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew the decrees of heaven. At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right."
Meng Yi asked what filial piety was. The Master said, "It is not being disobedient." Soon after, as Fan Chi was driving him, the Master told him, saying, "Mengsun asked me what filial piety was, and I answered him, 'not being disobedient.'" Fan Chi said, "What did you mean?" The Master replied, "That parents, when alive, should be served according to propriety; that, when dead, they should be buried according to propriety; and that they should be sacrificed to according to propriety."
Meng Wu asked what filial piety was. The Master said, "Parents are anxious lest their children should be sick."
Ziyou asked what filial piety was. The Master said, "The filial piety of nowadays means the support of one's parents. But dogs and horses likewise are able to do something in the way of support—without reverence, what is there to distinguish the one support given from the other?"
Zixia asked what filial piety was. The Master said, "The difficulty is with the countenance. If, when their elders have any troublesome affairs, the young take the toil of them, and if, when the young have wine and food, they set them before their elders, is this to be considered filial piety?"
The Master said, "I have talked with Hui for a whole day, and he has not made any objection to anything I said—as if he were stupid. He has retired, and I have examined his conduct when away from me, and found him able to illustrate my teachings. Hui—He is not stupid."
The Master said, "See what a person does. Mark one's motives. Examine in what things one rests. How can a person conceal one's character! How can a person conceal one's character!"
The Master said, "If a person keeps cherishing one's old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, one may be a teacher of others."
The Master said, "The accomplished scholar is not a utensil."
Zigong asked what constituted the superior person. The Master said, "One acts before one speaks, and afterwards speaks according to one's actions."
The Master said, "The superior person is catholic and no partisan. The mean person is a partisan and not catholic."
The Master said, "Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous."
The Master said, "The study of strange doctrines is injurious indeed!"
The Master said, "You, shall I teach you what knowledge is? When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it—this is knowledge."
Zizhang was learning with a view to official emolument. The Master said, "Hear much and put aside the points of which you stand in doubt, while you speak cautiously at the same time of the others—then you will afford few occasions for blame. See much and put aside the things which seem perilous, while you are cautious at the same time in carrying the others into practice—then you will have few occasions for repentance. When one gives few occasions for blame in one's words, and few occasions for repentance in one's conduct, one is in the way to get emolument."
Duke Ai asked, saying, "What should be done in order to secure the submission of the people?" Confucius replied, "Advance the upright and set aside the crooked, then the people will submit. Advance the crooked and set aside the upright, then the people will not submit."
Ji Kang asked how to cause the people to reverence their ruler, to be faithful to one, and to urge themselves to virtue. The Master said, "Let one preside over them with gravity—then they will reverence one. Let one be filial and kind to all—then they will be faithful to one. Let one advance the good and teach the incompetent—then they will eagerly seek to be virtuous."
Someone addressed Confucius, saying, "Sir, why are you not engaged in the government?" The Master said, "What does the Shujing say of filial piety? 'You are filial, you discharge your congenial duties. These qualities are displayed in government.' This then also constitutes the exercise of government. Why must there be THAT to make one be in the government?"
The Master said, "I do not know how a person without truthfulness is to get on. How can a large carriage be made to go without the crossbar for yoking the oxen to, or a small carriage without the arrangement for yoking the horses?"
Zizhang asked whether the affairs of ten ages after could be known. Confucius said, "The Yin dynasty followed the regulations of the Xia: wherein it took from or added to them may be known. The Zhou dynasty has followed the regulations of the Yin: wherein it took from or added to them may be known. Some other may follow the Zhou, but though it should be at the distance of a hundred ages, its affairs may be known."
The Master said, "For a person to sacrifice to a spirit which does not belong to one is flattery. To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage."

龟奶奶算着，聚宝盆生出来的钱，宋元通宝，能买好多饼子、馍馍、馒头、面条……再不用给老幺喝稀粥啦。对了，麦子也收了，给盈盈和老幺，都攒点买地钱。
也不能都攒着，老幺要是回来啊，就买点——

Granny Turtle checked her Treasure Basin once again. Lately, a lot more coins have appeared inside it.
She asked around, and people told her they were Song Coins.
Oh... then these are good coins. With Song Coins, she could buy Yingying a new pair of shoes. The girl ran and skipped everywhere, and her shoes were all worn through... She could save a little for the eldest, too. No, no, the eldest hadn't come home yet, but the youngest had.
The youngest was a good child, always coming and going in a whirlwind. When that fierce-looking man barged in, it was the youngest who stood right in front of her and Yingying.
Granny Turtle calculated in her head. The coins from the Treasure Basin, these Song Coins, could buy so many things: flatbreads, steamed buns, rolls, noodles... The youngest would never have to live on thin gruel again. Ah, yes, the wheat had been harvested too. She should save a little toward buying land for both Yingying and the youngest.
But she couldn't just save it all. If the youngest came back, she ought to buy...
#YBig white steamed buns. The youngest was always dashing here and there with a sturdy build; only big buns would be filling enough and help them grow taller!#E

春寒，敬惟

敬竹林间的相遇，敬烈酒浇尽胸中块垒，敬并辔前行的游侠们，少年意气，一如既往。
天地浩荡，与君同往。
en:
Dear Wanderer,

As spring's chill lingers, we greet you with respect.

A wind stirs through the Bamboo Abode, with sword in hand, one steps into the world. Since the Young Master left the Bamboo Grove Abode, over #8c582330 million Wanderers#E have set foot on the Jianghu Journey, crossing fates amidst these rivers and mountains.

From the verdant hills of Qinghe to the bustling streets of Kaifeng, the Young Master has shed youthful naivety and begun to walk the true path of a warrior. So too has Yanyun grown alongside every Wanderer, refining every detail, striving to offer a better journey. This grand encounter we now share is thanks to your continuous support and patience. The road in the Jianghu is a difficult one to walk, yet our hearts remain sincere, and our fists, unwavering. All of us at Sixteen Lanes will continue to listen to your guidance and critique, repaying your trust with our utmost devotion. To show our gratitude, we offer #4d734da gift#E, a small gesture to express our heartfelt appreciation.

Here's to our meeting in the bamboo grove. To strong wine that drowns all burdens of the heart. To the Wanderers who ride side by side toward distant horizons, youthful spirit, ever the same.

The world is vast and boundless, we journey onward with you.

zh:
酒肆老板娘狄娟非但没有追究那日仓库醉酒一事，反倒请她在店里当了个帮工。
万无忧每日给客人拿酒斟酒，眼睛却偷偷地瞄着狄娟，和她吵架时飞起来的两撇眉毛。
她们是太不一样的人。爹娘说无忧是个窝里横，只敢对着家里人发脾气。而狄娟总把“谁能吵得赢我一个寡妇”挂在嘴边，可对狄福和无忧，却是百般周全。
有时候店里没什么客人，狄娟就给无忧说山外的事情，讲京城酒肆的飞天舞，讲神仙渡酒家的梨花香。无忧听着听着，忍不住想她是怎么带着孩子走南闯北，吃了多少苦，走了多少弯路，才到这晦谷里来，拉扯起酒旗，把千日醉的名声打响。
“只要酒好，到哪都能卖得出去。”狄娟的回答轻描淡写。
酒当然很好。闭店后无忧偷偷来到仓库旁，从墙角拿出一小壶自己藏起来的千日醉。怀着对老板娘的愧疚，以及对酒香的敬意，她轻轻抿了一口。
“……姐姐……能不能早点回家……睡不着……”
夜色里传来狄福的声音，吓得无忧一身酒气都散了不少。
“……好……小男子汉……”
这是狄娟的声音。
直爽洒脱的狄寡妇，原来是和她一般年纪的小姑娘。酒气蒸得无忧的脸又红又烫，她无意间发现了狄娟姐弟的小秘密。无忧觉得自己和老板娘的距离更近了一些。
en:
Di Juan didn't scold her. She hired her.
From then on, Wuyou fetched and poured wine for customers, though her eyes often drifted to Di Juan, especially when the woman argued, those sharp brows flying like drawn blades.
They couldn't have been more different. Wuyou's parents said she was only fierce at home, brave enough to snap at family and no one else. Di Juan liked to boast that no one could out-argue a widow. But with Di Fu and Wuyou, she was careful in every way that mattered.
On slow days, Di Juan told stories of the world beyond the valley: dancing girls who seemed to fly in capital taverns, pear-blossom wine perfuming riverside inns. Wuyou listened and wondered, how far had Di Juan traveled, how much hardship had she swallowed, to end up here, raising a wine banner and making Sweet Slumber a name people remembered?
"Good wine sells itself," Di Juan said lightly. "Wherever you pour it."
And the wine was good. After closing, Wuyou sneaked to the warehouse, fished out the small jug she'd hidden. With half guilty, half reverent in her heart, she took a careful sip.
"...Sis... come home early... can't sleep..."
Di Fu's voice drifted out of the dark, jolting most of the wine haze right out of her.
"... Alright... you brave little man..."
Di Juan's reply was softer than Wuyou had ever heard.
So the bold, unrestrained Widow Di was a girl not much older than herself. Heat crept up Wuyou's cheeks. She'd stumbled onto a secret, and somehow that made the distance between them feel smaller.

zh:
很少有人知道寄棺主二人并非主仆，实是一对父子。他父子二人本是世代豪强，因为不慎被绣金楼掳去改造成了梦傀。幸运的是他二人并未失去意识，然而不幸的是儿子筋骨尽断，只得寄居棺材，父亲无法说话，成了哑巴。由于外人只能听见棺材里的人说话指挥扛棺材的人，误以为二人是主仆，这才得名寄棺主。

寄棺主一直不愿成为绣金楼的傀儡，此番利用绣金楼入侵清河之机，父子二人合力，终于杀了出来。父亲一路扛着儿子，击退追兵，最终躲进一处绣金楼弃置实验材料的棺材堆。父子二人一直想尝试用弃置的材料为儿子恢复身体，可惜始终没有成功。

夜深人静时，寄棺主会问守在棺材旁的父亲：“我还想和您一同牵狗骑马打猎，有可能吗？”父亲无言，只默默抚着棺材。
en:
Few know the truth about the Coffin Keeper Lord. They are not master and servant—but father and son. Once a proud and powerful duo, the two were captured by Aureate Pavilion and forcibly remade into Sleeping Puppets. By some rare stroke of fortune, they managed to retain their consciousness. Unfortunately, the son's bones were shattered beyond repair, leaving him to live confined within a coffin, while the father lost his voice, becoming mute. To outsiders, it seemed as though the voice inside the coffin was giving commands to its bearer. Thus, they were named the Coffin Keeper Lord.

Yet the two of them never accepted their fate as Aureate Pavilion's puppets. Taking advantage of the chaos during Aureate Pavilion's invasion of Qinghe, they fought their way out to freedom. Carrying his son on his back, the father fended off wave after wave of pursuers, finally escaping to a heap of abandoned coffins once used for failed experiments. Since then, they have tried again and again to rebuild the son's body using discarded materials, but success has always eluded them.

In the deep of night, when all is silent, the son sometimes asks from within the coffin:

"Father, do you think we could ever ride horses, walk dogs, and hunt together again like we used to?"

His father says nothing. He merely rests a weathered hand on the coffin's lid, and remains by his side in silence.

太仓粟曾于八载之前，深罹毒疫之祸。隐雾林畔达安村受害尤烈。幸得青溪医者竭力施治，方将毒菌遏于雾林之中。然，近日那祸根毒菌，竟又再现人间。
至达安村中，只见雾气缭绕，街巷空寂，院落无声。唯有一怪物背影，忽隐忽现。细加探查，方觉村民似有意遮掩某不可告人之秘。诸般线索，皆指向村中祠堂。几经波折，终得祠堂之钥。未料，毒菌已覆满祠堂四壁。
轻触祠堂牌位，忽而神思恍惚，陷入一段不知是何人的记忆。由此，方知荒村之由来，及一段绵延十二载的恩怨情仇。
en:
Eight years ago, Granary of Plenty was ravaged by a deadly plague. Sorrowfield Village by Mistveil Forest suffered the worst, saved only by the strenuous efforts of the Silver Needle doctors, who contained the poisonous fungus within Mistveil Forest.
Arriving at Sorrowfield Village, mist shrouds the air, streets lie empty, and courtyards stand silent. Only the shadowy figure of a monster flickers in and out of view. Closer inspection reveals villagers seem to hide a dark secret, all clues pointing to the village shrine. After much effort, the shrine’s key is obtained, revealing walls overgrown with poisonous fungus.
Touching a memorial tablet in the shrine triggers a trance, unveiling the origins of this forsaken village and a twelve-year saga of love and hate.

zh:
猫本没有名字。吃的鱼多了，也就该有名字了。
钓鱼人们最钟爱鲤鲤这只小猫咪。鲤鲤只有拳头大的时候，就认得钓鱼的人们。它乖巧地蹲在钓鱼人旁边，和他们静静地一起等。
人们很稀奇，便给鲤鲤丢小鱼吃。就在这时，大家发现了这只小猫鲜明的兴趣：永远先吃锦鲤。
黑的白的、金的花的、大的小的，只要丢给鲤鲤，它准能从一大堆鱼里精准挑出来，叼到一旁先吃掉。
鲤鱼多刺，人们担心鲤鲤卡骨头，便蹲在它旁边看它吃。
鲤鲤才不要人担心。猫有锋利的爪子，有尖尖的牙齿。猫天生就能对付多刺的鱼！
当人们看见鲤鲤献宝似的把剔出的完美鱼骨往前一推，他们就知道这猫天生就是对付锦鲤的。
人有一种说法，缺什么，名字里就叫什么。一只小猫从此有了鱼的名字。
en:
A cat doesn't need a name, not really. But after eating enough fish, one might just earn one.
That's how it was with Finny. Even when she was no bigger than a fist, she'd sit quietly by the fishermen, patient as a stone.
Amused, they'd toss her small fish. That's when they noticed her peculiar taste: she would always, always pick out the brocade carp first.
From a heap of silvery catch, she'd find the gold and white, the spotted and red, and carry them off to eat in private.
Worried she'd choke on the bones, they'd watch her.
They needn't have bothered. With the precision of a born hunter, she'd lay down a perfect, clean-picked skeleton as if presenting a gift.
And so, a little cat without a name was given one: Finny.

卷一：天虫本源
夫“蚕”字，上天而下虫，本乎天外。蚕母者，肇始太虚，吐丝、结茧、破蜕，顺天理而流转，超然物外。
千载前，神威初降江左，先民有幸，得窥神迹。先秦古俗，多以重重丝帛束裹死者入土，盖期亡魂效法蚕母，得道飞升也。

卷二：神踪可循
千载以降，蚕母真身早绝于红尘。然神踪虽隐，残响尚存。试举三证以明之。
一为蚕事之广。九州浩瀚，万里相隔，却于多地同兴蚕桑、共铸奉蚕之器。此乃天地生灵共沐蚕母神通之明证。
二为闭关之法。后世释、道诸教，皆有“闭关静修”之说，绝水米、净六根，以期超凡入圣。此法何来？实乃先民亲见天虫不食不动、茧中化水、破壳而飞之后，以己身效之。所谓闭关者，人自造茧也。
三为天子蚕祭。历代帝王不惜屈万乘之尊，岁岁亲祭先蚕。世人只道是祈农桑丰收，然帝王之祭，何曾为稻粱谋？先蚕祭之本质，乃天子代万民叩问蚕母造化之仪。

卷三：脱胎换骨
故知吾辈奉蚕母之要，在脱胎换骨。
血肉之躯，终有生老病死。灵魂困于其中，如蚕困于茧壳，纵有冲天之志，终不得飞。
然蚕母以天虫示道：彼小虫尚能羽化飞升，何况人乎？
循此道者当明：褪尽凡胎劣骨，方为挣脱皮囊之狱，使魂魄得白日飞升。蜕者，非失乃得。
所变非人，乃超乎人上。
en:
Scroll One: The Origin of the Heavenly Worm
Now, the character for "silkworm" is formed of "heaven" above and "worm" below, its origin lying beyond the heavens themselves. The Silkworm Mother arose at the dawn of the Great Void, spinning silk, weaving her cocoon, and breaking free from it, following the course of heavenly principle, transcendent beyond all worldly things.
A thousand years ago, divine might first descended upon the lands east of the river, and the ancients were fortunate enough to glimpse this sacred trace. In the customs of high antiquity, the dead were often wrapped in layer upon layer of silk cloth before burial, in the hope that their departed souls might emulate the Silkworm Mother, attain the Way, and ascend on wings.

Scroll Two: Traces of the Divine, Still to Be Found
In the thousand years since, the true form of the Silkworm Mother has long vanished from the mortal world. Yet though her divine traces lie hidden, faint echoes still remain. Let three proofs be offered to illuminate this truth.
The first is the breadth of sericulture itself. Across the vastness of the Nine Provinces, though separated by ten thousand li, sericulture and mulberry cultivation flourished alike in many lands, and vessels for honoring the silkworm were cast in common. This stands as clear proof that all living creatures beneath heaven and earth were bathed alike in the Silkworm Mother's divine magic.
The second is the method of seclusion. In later ages, both the schools of Buddhism and Daoism speak of "seclusion for quiet cultivation"—abstaining from water and grain, purifying the six senses, in hope of transcending the mundane and attaining sagehood. Whence came this method? It was born of the ancients, who, having witnessed with their own eyes the heavenly worm neither eating nor moving, dissolving into liquid within its cocoon, then breaking free to take flight, sought to emulate it with their own bodies. What is called seclusion is but a cocoon that man weaves for himself.
The third is the Emperor's silkworm rite. Throughout the ages, emperors have not begrudged bending their ten-thousand-chariot dignity to personally offer sacrifice to the First Silkworm, year upon year. The world believes this merely a prayer for bountiful harvests of grain and mulberry—yet when has an emperor's sacrifice ever truly been for rice and millet? The true essence of the First Silkworm Rite is a ceremony wherein the Emperor, on behalf of all his people, beseeches the Silkworm Mother for the secret of transformation.

Scroll Three: Shedding the Mortal Frame
Thus we know: the essence of honoring the Silkworm Mother lies in shedding the mortal frame and remaking the bones.
The body of flesh and blood must in the end know birth, age, sickness, and death. The soul, trapped within it, is as the silkworm trapped within its cocoon—though it harbors ambitions to pierce the very heavens, in the end it cannot take flight.
Yet the Silkworm Mother has shown us the Way through the heavenly worm: if even so small a creature can achieve metamorphosis and ascend on wings, how much more so may man?
Those who follow this path must understand: only by shedding the common flesh and inferior bone entirely can one break free from the prison of the mortal husk, and let the soul ascend in broad daylight. To molt is not to lose, but to gain.
What one becomes is no longer human—it is something that transcends humanity itself.
Xi Shu

zh:
【国风·魏风】

葛屦

纠纠葛屦，可以履霜。掺掺女手，可以缝裳。要之襋之，好人服之。
好人提提，宛然左辟，佩其象揥。维是𥚹心，是以为刺。

汾沮洳

彼汾沮洳，言采其莫。彼其之子，美无度。美无度，殊异乎公路。
彼汾一方，言采其桑。彼其之子，美如英。美如英，殊异乎公行。
彼汾一曲，言采其藚。彼其之子，美如玉。美如玉，殊异乎公族。

园有桃

园有桃，其实之殽。心之忧矣，我歌且谣。不知我者，谓我士也骄。彼人是哉，子曰何其？心之忧矣，其谁知之？其谁知之，盖亦勿思。
园有棘，其实之食。心之忧矣，聊以行国。不知我者，谓我士也罔极。彼人是哉，子曰何其？心之忧矣，其谁知之？其谁知之，盖亦勿思。

陟岵

陟彼岵兮，瞻望父兮。父曰嗟予子，行役夙夜无已。上慎旃哉！犹来无止。
陟彼屺兮，瞻望母兮。母曰嗟予季，行役夙夜无寐。上慎旃哉！犹来无弃。
陟彼冈兮，瞻望兄兮。兄曰嗟予弟，行役夙夜必偕。上慎旃哉！犹来无死。

十亩之间

十亩之间兮，桑者闲闲兮，行与子还兮。
十亩之外兮，桑者泄泄兮，行与子逝兮。

伐檀

坎坎伐檀兮，置之河之干兮，河水清且涟猗。不稼不穑，胡取禾三百廛兮？不狩不猎，胡瞻尔庭有县貆兮？彼君子兮，不素餐兮！
坎坎伐辐兮，置之河之侧兮，河水清且直猗。不稼不穑，胡取禾三百亿兮？不狩不猎，胡瞻尔庭有县特兮？彼君子兮，不素食兮！
坎坎伐轮兮，置之河之漘兮，河水清且沦猗。不稼不穑，胡取禾三百囷兮？不狩不猎，胡瞻尔庭有县鹑兮？彼君子兮，不素飧兮！

硕鼠

硕鼠硕鼠，无食我黍。三岁贯女，莫我肯顾。逝将去女，适彼乐土。乐土乐土，爰得我所！
硕鼠硕鼠，无食我麦。三岁贯女，莫我肯德。逝将去女，适彼乐国。乐国乐国，爰得我直！
硕鼠硕鼠，无食我苗。三岁贯女，莫我肯劳。逝将去女，适彼乐郊。乐郊乐郊，谁之永号！
en:
【Airs of the States · Airs of Wei】

Straw Sandals

Straw sandals, well-woven, can tread on frost. A maiden's slender hands can sew a robe. The waist and collar are made, for a fine lady to wear.
The fine lady steps gracefully, turning aside to the left, wearing her ivory hairpin. Her heart is narrow, thus this is made as a satire.

By the Fen Riverside

By the marshy Fen riverside, I gather the shepherd's purse. That man, so handsome beyond measure. Handsome beyond measure, unlike the Duke's officer.
By the Fen riverside, I gather mulberry leaves. That man, handsome as a flower. Handsome as a flower, unlike the Duke's attendant.
By a bend of the Fen, I gather the water-plantain. That man, handsome as jade. Handsome as jade, unlike the Duke's clansman.

In the Garden is a Peach Tree

In the garden is a peach tree, its fruit is food. My heart is troubled, I sing and chant. Those who do not know me say, "This scholar is arrogant." Are those men right? What do you say? My heart is troubled, who knows it? Who knows it? Why not just not think?
In the garden is a jujube tree, its fruit is food. My heart is troubled, I wander through the state. Those who do not know me say, "This scholar knows no bounds." Are those men right? What do you say? My heart is troubled, who knows it? Who knows it? Why not just not think?

Climbing the Hill

I climb that wooded hill, gazing towards my father. Father says, "Alas, my son, on service day and night without rest. Be careful up there! May you return and not stay."
I climb that bare hill, gazing towards my mother. Mother says, "Alas, my youngest, on service day and night without sleep. Be careful up there! May you return and not be abandoned."
I climb that ridge, gazing towards my elder brother. Brother says, "Alas, my younger brother, on service day and night always together. Be careful up there! May you return and not die."

Within Ten Acres

Within ten acres, the mulberry pickers are leisurely. I will go home with you.
Beyond ten acres, the mulberry pickers are relaxed. I will go away with you.

Chopping Sandalwood

Clank, clank we chop sandalwood, place it by the river's bank, the river water clear with ripples. You sow not nor reap, why take three hundred sheaves of grain? You hunt not nor chase, why see badgers hanging in your court? Those gentlemen, they do not eat the bread of idleness!
Clank, clank we chop for spokes, place it by the river's side, the river water clear and straight. You sow not nor reap, why take three hundred million grains? You hunt not nor chase, why see boars hanging in your court? Those gentlemen, they do not eat the food of idleness!
Clank, clank we chop for wheels, place it by the river's brink, the river water clear with eddies. You sow not nor reap, why take three hundred granaries of grain? You hunt not nor chase, why see quails hanging in your court? Those gentlemen, they do not eat the supper of idleness!

Big Rat

Big rat, big rat, do not eat my millet. Three years I've served you, yet you show me no care. I am going to leave you, for that happy land. Happy land, happy land, where I shall find my place!
Big rat, big rat, do not eat my wheat. Three years I've served you, yet you show me no kindness. I am going to leave you, for that happy state. Happy state, happy state, where I shall get my due!
Big rat, big rat, do not eat my seedlings. Three years I've served you, yet you show me no comfort. I am going to leave you, for those happy borders. Happy borders, happy borders, who will there long lament!

zh:
藏下这份银子时，你也跟了我好些年了。眼看着你从一个小不点窜成了个比我还高的小伙，看来“小钱串”这个诨名起得不错，果真和我的钱串子一样，越串越长条了。

如今小钱串长成了大钱串，也该像我钱多多一般有个响当当的大名了。
那日你来问我，就随掌柜的姓，叫钱池子如何，听着也很有钱……死脑筋，真不懂变通！你对算账无甚兴趣，还那般喜欢骑马，干啥子非要跟着我起名字？
依我看，“驰”倒是个好字，所以偷偷写了藏你枕头下了，也不知你发没发现。

素日里你总说掌柜的待你抠门儿，月钱少得可怜。嗐，一看就是年轻——我那是教你存钱呢！
我开的月钱可比外头那些老爷多多了，拿到手里看着少，不过是给你记着来日的康健保金、屋业积金、颐养休金……积累要趁早，将来才好钱生钱，一生无忧嘛！

罢了，等你看到这封信时，大抵我也老了，你也有了自己的名号。届时你若成了名，又得了这笔横财，记着仔细来谢谢我的好主意，更不许再说我抠门儿了！

（另一张纸上密密麻麻地记着小钱串的每月月钱，岁岁有增长，更有不少掌柜的额外补贴，一直记到了其百年之后。）
en:
By the time I hid away this silver, you had already been with me for years. I watched you grow from a tiny little thing into a fine young man taller than I am. It seems "Little Coin" was a fitting nickname all along. Just like my strings of coins, you kept growing longer by the year.

Now that you are all grown, you need a proper name to match, just as I, Qian Duoduo, have one of my own. That day when you came to ask me about it, you said perhaps you should take the shopkeeper's surname and call yourself Qian Chizi. Rich enough by the sound of it, you said. Stubborn boy. Not a bit of flexibility in you. You never cared much for keeping accounts, and were always fonder of riding horses. Why insist on taking a name after me?
To my mind, Chi is a fine character, so I secretly wrote it down and tucked it beneath your pillow. Whether you ever found it, I couldn't say.

You were always saying your shopkeeper was too stingy with you, that your monthly wages were pitifully small. Hah. That only showed how green you still were. I was teaching you to save.
What I gave you was more generous than what you would have gotten anywhere else. It only looked like less in your hand because I had already set part of it aside for you. Money for sickness, money for a house, money for your old age. One must start saving early, so that money may in time make more money, and a man may go through life free of worry.

Enough. By the time you read this letter, I expect I will already be old, and you will have made a name for yourself. When that day comes, if fame is yours and this windfall has also fallen into your hands, remember to thank me properly for my foresight. And do not call me stingy ever again.

(Another sheet is covered edge to edge in cramped writing, recording Little Coin's monthly wages. The sum rises year by year, with many extra allowances added by the shopkeeper out of pocket, and the accounts continue on for a full hundred years to come.)

zh:
比起身死的李筠，被囚于锁链之中的慕容延钊，石守信似乎是结局最为体面之人，他没有在战场上丢了命，也没有在锁链中失了魂。不过是从地面的将军，成了暗中的执手。
他比慕容延钊杀得果断，也比李筠更识时务，他知道，人注定抓不住一本要翻页的册子，赵匡胤是那册子上写好的下一页，但他的朋友却不明白，还死死地捉住过去的故事，直到满手皆是墨汁，太蠢，实在太蠢。

最初，他回不去石家村，没有见过爹娘，听说娘盼着他回来，纵使他是千夫所指的叛徒，还是心疼他。
后来，他的身边又少了几位朋友，有些人问他值不值，有些人说他聪明，有些人托孤给他。
再后来，他手中亦没有了兵权，堪堪换来了一条性命，有人说他失势，有人说他审时度势。
他是个聪明人？还是个蠢人？

这种事情问自己是问不出来的，没有人会觉得自己做的是蠢事，否则为何会去做呢。
也许之后会有万千的骂名在他的身上，但美名已死之人听不清，骂名已死之人亦听不见，美名和骂名也没有什么关系，这样的声音他不想听，听起来也并无用处。

他站在武庙之外，耳边是工匠往来的脚步声，炎炎烈日砸在他们的脊背之上，再被他们的号子喝破，这才是当下的声音，那朝堂之上的帝王的言语，那才是当下的声音，石家村滔天的洪水，旧友的呢喃，在今日的日光下，似乎已经变得极浅。
en:
Compared to Li Jun, who died in battle, and Murong Yanzhao, now shackled in chains, Shi Shouxin's fate seemed the most dignified. No life lost on the battlefield, no soul broken in captivity. He merely stepped from the light of generalship into the shadows of power.
He struck more decisively than Murong Yanzhao, adapted more shrewdly than Li Jun. He understood: one cannot cling to a book whose pages are destined to turn. Zhao Kuangyin was the next chapter, written in ink long dried. But his friends refused to see it, gripping the past until their hands were stained black with futility. Fools. Utter fools.

At first, he couldn't return to Shi Family Village or see his parents. He heard his mother still longed for him. Even though he was reviled as a traitor, she still ached for her son.
Then, he lost more friends. Some asked if his choices were worth it, some called him clever, some entrusted their children to him.
Later, he relinquished his military power, barely securing his life. Some said he'd fallen from grace, others praised his ability to "judge the situation".
Was he a wise man or a fool?

Such questions couldn't be answered by looking inward. No one thinks their own actions are foolish, otherwise, why take them?
Perhaps endless curses would follow him, but he couldn't hear the praises of the dead, nor the insults. Praise and scorn were irrelevant now. He didn't care to listen. Such voices served no purpose.

Standing outside the Martial Temple, his ears filled with the footsteps of artisans, their backs bent under the scorching sun, their work chants shattering the heat. These were the sounds of the present. The emperor's words in the court chambers, those were the sounds of the present. The floodwaters of Shi Family Village, the whispers of old friends, under today's sun, had faded to near nothing.

听闻你的建议，佛手郎开怀一笑，大张将军也欣然允诺。
en:
The Governor's Residence blazes with lantern light and festal colors, where a magnificent victory banquet is currently underway. General Zhang Huaishen has returned from his campaign, and General Zhang Yichao is about to return to the Tang court. The feast is meant not only to honor the army, but also to reassure the people of Liangzhou and set their hearts at ease. And yet, though the hall is crowded with guests, the two generals themselves are nowhere to be seen. You find your way to the Buddha Hand's study, where the two of them sit facing one another at the desk, seemingly deep in discussion. You are still hesitating over whether to disturb them when the Buddha Hand looks up, drops his brush, and, with easy warmth, slips an arm around your shoulders, urging you to join them. General Zhang Yichao also inclines his head in greeting.
In this gathering, you have thousands of words in your heart, yet no idea where to begin. At this moment, you simply want to...
#Y[Invite them to watch the snow atop Wuwei Mountain.] That was where you first met the Buddha Hand. Did General Zhang Yichao ever behold such a scene in his younger days? At the beginning of the journey, fine snow rested on your shoulders as you stood together admiring the view; at the end of the story, frost and ice would cover the prefectural city, and only silence would remain among their tombs.#E
Hearing your suggestion, the Buddha's Hand laughs heartily, and General Zhang Yichao readily agrees.

长生的日子太平静了，说不定我们要在这渊底呆上一百年，我只能记录自己的生平打发时间。
我不是什么长生仙人，我只有一个名字，“巴梧”。
阿婆跟我说，“巴梧”的意思是“鹿神娘娘庇佑的孩子”，所以我要常年戴着鹿头面具，聆听娘娘的声音。
但我听其他人说，是因为我跟常人生得不一样，才必须用面具遮住头。
阿婆照料我长大，她屋子里有一只蟾王，方圆十里的毒虫每天都会爬过来，像供神那样将新鲜药草放在蟾王面前。蟾王很喜欢我，它是我的朋友。村子里传说我得了鹿神娘娘的庇佑，所有的毒虫都被我身体里的天音降服。
我的事传了出去，外面称我为“长生仙人”，阿婆绕着村子撒下药粉，说不能让外人找到这里，她一直在躲“江湖人”。
江湖是个好听的名字，可我们就是因为江湖人才掉到渊底，只能长生。
眼下唯一的希望，只有陈怀卿的方子了。
能让大家摆脱长生的方子。
en:
Immortality is tediously quiet. We might be stuck at the bottom of this abyss for a hundred years, and all I can do to pass the time is write down my own story.
I'm no Immortal of Longevity. I am but a man named Ba Wu.
Granny told me "Ba Wu" means "child blessed by the Deer Goddess," so I've worn a deer mask all my life, straining to hear her whispers.
But others say the mask is meant to hide how different I look.
Granny raised me in a hut shared with the Toad King. Every day, venomous swarms from miles around would crawl to it, bearing fresh herbs at its feet like offering tribute. The Toad King liked me. It was my only friend. The villagers believed the Deer Goddess had truly blessed me, that the poison in my veins could subdue any venom.
Word spread, and outsiders branded me "the Immortal of Longevity." Granny scattered herb powder around the village, warning that we must never be found. She was hiding from some wanderers.
Jianghu, or the martial world, sounds poetic. But it was because of the wanderers that we fell into this abyss, cursed with this endless life.
Our only hope now lies with Chen Huaiqing's formula.
The one that might free us from longevity.
One... two... three...

zh:
《田螺公子》

身为一名狂澜弟子，谢钦和同门略有差别。
狂澜酩酊痛饮时，哪怕酒水打湿衣衫，也是潇洒恣意。
而他会用皂角泡好衣服，然后在酒渍处仔细搓洗，天气晴好多加晾晒。
同门举起酒坛轮流一人一口的时候，他就要尴尬不失礼貌地笑笑：婉拒了哈。
简而言之，他有洁癖。

他自信胸有铮铮铁骨，生死无意，长枪为冢。
但——喜欢干净没有错！身为狂澜弟子喜欢干净也没有错！
他在心里这样大喊，将自己攒了多年的银钱，置下一间偏僻小院。
闯荡江湖回来，还能打扫庭院，种种花草。
毕竟有人对他说过，好好活着，这笔账就算清了。

这日归家，他那窗明几净，一尘不染的小院门口，却躺着个脏兮兮的人。
与其说人，还不如说是块破破烂烂的抹布。
谢钦头皮发麻，伸手俯身探了探鼻息——还活着。
凭借着从军时学到的些微医术，抹布从鬼门关捡回一条命。

这人梳洗得干干净净，刚有点力气说话就开始鬼话连篇。
“啥叫鬼话？我真是开封巨富于家的儿子！因嫡庶之争被歹人陷害，你遇上我正是发达的好时机，给我五十两银子，我还你一个未来！”
“瞒不住了，我是官府派来的，缉捕坏人时不慎遗失腰牌。给我五十两银子，帮你把事儿平了！”

每周某日，都能听到这样的鬼话，仿佛是什么疯狂的节日庆典。
谢钦索性堵上耳朵，只道伤好了之后，随他去哪。
“于公子”堪堪能下地拄着拐杖走路的时候，家门口来了几个人。
谢钦把家里值钱的东西都交了出去。

“便宜他们还不如便宜我呢……”于公子怒问，“你到底欠了什么？”
谢钦指着架子上的一坛酒。狂澜门下，酒肉生死都是账。饮酒赔命，欠命还酒。
我欠人一条命，这壶酒却没机会还了。

谢钦看懂了他的眼神：“你不欠我。” 举手之劳，只是不想见人落入泥沼。
次日，于公子像变了个人。
虽然腿伤未愈，走路东摇西晃，但扫地做饭样样抢着来，令谢钦摸不着头脑。
“因为……我乃天汉中白水素仙，上天悯你，命我前来相助。懂了就给我五十两银子……”
谢钦差点没拿稳筷子。
洁癖自是无药可救，但有人陪着用餐，却另有一番暖意。

天气转凉，于公子伤势大好，生龙活虎。
他对谢钦的谢客暗示视而不见，外出几天又大大咧咧回到小院，如入无人之境。
直到这日，谢钦对他说：“这院子已抵给他人，明日起不必再来。”
他的酒没法还给战场上死去的兄弟，将微薄田产赠予在世亲人，也算弥补。

于公子不管不顾，非要借宿一晚。
次日，那坛酒和这人，都消失得无影无踪，只留下一枚“是利封”。

谢钦收拾行囊去了开封，为找酒，也为谋生。
“既然被你抓住了，酒还你。” 被生擒的那天，于公子分外开怀：“别看我这样，也是有恩必报，有报必报不完的义侠！”
谢钦只是冷笑。酒还了，其他呢？
“不如……先告诉我你的真名。”
en:
The Diligent Housekeeper 

Xie Qin, a Raging Tides disciple, was unlike most of his peers. 
While others drank deeply and carelessly, often soaking their clothes with wine without a second thought, Xie took a different approach. 
He carefully washed his garments with soap pods, scrubbing out every stain and drying them thoroughly under the sun on clear days. 
When his fellow disciples raised the wine jar for a round, each taking a sip, he would politely but awkwardly decline, saying, "I'll pass this time." 
In short, he was a neat freak. 

He carried himself with unwavering resolve, fearless in the face of life and death, wielding his spear as though it were his own tombstone. 
But there was no shame in wanting cleanliness, he told himself firmly. Even a Raging Tides disciple could value order and purity. 
With that conviction, he saved every coin meticulously, eventually purchasing a quiet, secluded courtyard. 
After a long life roaming the jianghu, he dreamed of returning home, tending the garden, and nurturing flowers. 
Someone once told him: to live well was to settle all scores. 

One day, returning home, he found something lying at the pristine gate of his courtyard— 
a filthy, ragged figure that was more a tattered cloth than a person. 
A chill ran down Xie's spine as he leaned down and checked for breath. The figure was alive. 
Drawing on his modest medical knowledge from his days in the army, he gently pulled this lost soul back from the edge of death. 

Once cleaned and slightly recovered, the stranger began babbling incessantly—nonsensical words spilling out like a broken river. 
"What nonsense is this? I am truly the son of the wealthy Yu family of Kaifeng! Wrongfully accused in a family dispute, meeting me is your lucky chance. Give me fifty taels of silver, and I promise a bright future for you." 
"I can no longer keep up the pretense—I was sent by the authorities. Lost my badge while pursuing criminals. Give me fifty taels, and I'll make everything right for you." 

Every week, on a certain day, voices echo with such incredible stories, as if a wild festival were taking place. 
Xie simply covered his ears, thinking that once his wound healed, he would go wherever he wished. 
When "Young Master Yu" was barely able to walk with a cane, a few visitors arrived at the gate. 
Xie handed over all the valuables from the house. 

"It's better to settle with me than with them," Young Master Yu said angrily. "What exactly do you owe?" 
Xie pointed to a jar of wine on the shelf. In the Raging Tides, debts between life and death are settled with wine and flesh. Drinking may cost a life; a life-draining debt may be repaid with wine. 
"I owe someone a life, but this jar of wine will never be used to repay that debt." 

Noticing the look in Young Master Yu's eyes, Xie added, "You don't owe me anything." It was a small kindness, done simply to keep someone from sinking deeper into hardship. 
The next day, Young Master Yu seemed transformed. 
Though his leg was still healing and his steps unsteady, he eagerly took up every task—from sweeping the floor to cooking—leaving Xie puzzled. 
"Because... I am an immortal. Heaven has taken pity on you and sent me to help. Understood? Now, give me fifty taels of silver..." 
Xie nearly fumbled his chopsticks. 
His cleanliness obsession was a hopeless habit, yet sharing a meal with someone brought an unexpected warmth. 

As the days grew colder, Young Master Yu's injuries healed swiftly, and he regained his spirited vigor. 
He paid no attention to Xie's subtle hints to leave, wandering in and out of the courtyard as though it were his own domain. 
Until one day, Xie spoke firmly, "This courtyard has been promised to another. Don't come back after tomorrow." 
Unable to repay the wine he owed to his fallen peers on the battlefield, Xie had instead bequeathed his modest family land to his living kin, hoping to find some peace in that. 

Young Master Yu dismissed all this, insisting on staying just one more night. 
By morning, both the wine and the man had disappeared without a trace, leaving behind only a sealed letter. 

With a heavy heart, Xie packed his belongings and set out for Kaifeng—both to recover the lost wine and to seek a new path. 
"Since you've caught me, I'll return the wine," Young Master Yu had said with a bright smile the day he was captured. "Don't judge me by appearances—I'm a man of honor who repays every kindness, endlessly." 
Xie gave a cold laugh. The wine was returned, but what of the rest? 
"Perhaps... you'd start by telling me your true name."

前言：文津馆有一弟子，名孔调，常立于寝庐中央论消暑之道，故人称“中央孔调”。其室友辑录其言，编纂成册，谓之《调语》，以解众人暑热之燥。

——正文——

调曰：学而食炸鸡，不亦热乎？五人睡一间房，不亦更热乎？人不冰而不愠，不亦心止乎？

调曰：天将降大任于斯人也，必先烤其心智，挠其筋骨，热其体肤，焦灼其身，行拂乱其所为，所以动心忍性，增益其所不能！

调曰：三人寝，必有我湿焉。择其汗少者而远之，其汗多者而踢之。
有舍友问曰：汝敢踢我之？不惧伤和气乎？
调曰：暑热之时，和气相蒸，凉之可也。
又问：若人皆汗多，岂非汝踢我、我踢汝乎？
调曰：然。互踢，则皆凉。

调曰：饭热食饮热水，曲肱而枕之，汗亦在其中矣。

调曰：汗，取之于身，而咸于身。冰，水为之，而化于暑。

......
en:
Preface: There is a disciple of Inkbound Order named Ai Kong, who often stood in the center of his dormitory chamber discoursing on the ways of dispelling summer heat, and thus was called by others "Central Ai." His roommates compiled his sayings into a volume, calling it "Full of Ai," to relieve the restlessness of all who suffer the summer heat.

Ai said: To study and yet eat fried chicken, is this not hot indeed? For five men to sleep in one chamber, is this not hotter still? For a man not to be given ice and yet not resent it, is this not the stilling of the heart?

Ai said: When Heaven is about to confer a great task upon a man, it must first roast his mind and will, vex his sinews and bones, heat his flesh and skin, scorch his very body, and confound whatever he undertakes, so as to stir his heart and steel his patience, increasing what he could not before achieve!

Ai said: Among three men sleeping together, surely one is more drenched than me. Choose the one who sweats least and keep your distance from him; as for the one who sweats most, kick him away.
A roommate asked: Dare you kick me so? Do you not fear it will harm our harmony?
Ai said: In the heat of summer, harmony itself steams and simmers; to cool it is only proper.
He asked further: If all men sweat alike, then is it not simply you kicking me, and I kicking you?
Ai said: Just so. If each kicks the other, then both shall be cooled.

Ai said: To eat hot meals and drink hot water, bending one's arm as a pillow beneath the head... sweat, too, lies within this.

zh:
【颂·周颂】

清庙之什

清庙

於穆清庙，肃雝显相。
济济多士，秉文之德。
对越在天，骏奔走在庙。
不显不承，无射于人斯！

维天之命

维天之命，於穆不已。
於乎不显，文王之德之纯。
假以溢我，我其收之。
骏惠我文王，曾孙笃之。
……

臣工之什

臣工

嗟嗟臣工，敬尔在公。王厘尔成，来咨来茹。
嗟嗟保介，维莫之春，亦又何求？如何新畲？
於皇来牟，将受厥明。明昭上帝，迄用康年。
命我众人：庤乃钱镈，奄观铚艾。

噫嘻

噫嘻成王，既昭假尔。
率时农夫，播厥百谷。
骏发尔私，终三十里。
亦服尔耕，十千维耦。
……
闵予小子之什

闵予小子

闵予小子，遭家不造，嬛嬛在疚。
於乎皇考，永世克孝。
念兹皇祖，陟降庭止。
维予小子，夙夜敬止。
於乎皇王，继序思不忘。

访落

访予落止，率时昭考。
於乎悠哉，朕未有艾。
将予就之，继犹判涣。
维予小子，未堪家多难。
绍庭上下，陟降厥家。
休矣皇考，以保明其身。
……
en:
【Hymns of Zhou】

Decade of Qing Miao

Qing Miao

Oh, solemn and pure is the temple,
Reverent and harmonious are the illustrious assistants.
Great officers, in crowds,
Maintain the virtue of King Wen.
Responding to and praising him in heaven,
They hurry about in the temple.
Very illustrious, very gracious,
They are never weary of doing so!

Decree of Heaven

The decree of Heaven,
How profound and unceasing!
Oh, how glorious
Was the purity of the virtue of King Wen!
His gifts overflow upon us.
We will receive them,
Trusting in the favor of King Wen,
That it may be relied on for ever by his descendants.
……

Decade of Chen Gong

Chen Gong

Ah! ye ministers,
Be reverent, be careful,
In the discharge of your public duties.
The king has given you perfect rules;—
Consult about them, and consider them.
Ah! ye assistants,
It is now the end of spring;
And what have ye to seek for?
How do you proceed with your new fields?
How beautiful are the wheat and the barley,
Whose bright produce we shall receive!
The bright and glorious God
Will in them give us a good year.
Order all our men
To be provided with their spades and hoes;—
Anon we shall see the sickles at work.

Yi Xi

Alas!
Our king,
Has succeeded to his ancestors.
He leads all the husbandmen
To sow their various kinds of grain,
Quickly he is pushing his work
Over those thirty li;
He is engaged with you
In the business of your ploughing,
With his thousands of pairs,
Who remove the roots and the bushes.
……
Decade of Min Yu Xiao Zi

Min Yu Xiao Zi

Pity me, the little child,
On whom has devolved the unsettled state!
Solitary am I and full of distress.
Oh! my great Father,
All thy life long,
Thou wast filial.
Thou didst think of my great grandfather,
(Seeing him, as it were,) ascending and descending in the court.
I, the little child,
Day and night will be as reverent.
Oh! ye great kings,
As your successor, I will strive not to forget you.

Fang Luo

When I think of the commencement [of my duties],
[I follow] my illustrious father.
Alas! how [far-reaching] was his wisdom!
But I am a child, and without knowledge.
I will go on, and be helped [by him],
Continuing and developing [his plans].
I, the little child,
Am not equal to the many difficulties of the family.
I will go up and down,
In the court and in the house,
Assisted by my great father,
Who will preserve and enlighten me.
……

zh:
毛毡懒洋洋地张开眼，不情不愿挪动了一下屁股。
崇德殿的广场东边是它最喜欢的角落，在这里能享受到冬天下午暖暖的阳光。
不知不觉，阳光已经转到了另一边。毛毡追随着暖意，继续躺倒。
这处宫殿隔几天会热闹一阵。那时候毛毡会躲到树丛里，看着不同颜色衣衫的人进殿出殿。
有人脚步轻快，好像乘了能飞上天的风一般。有人叹气沉重，呼吸里沉淀着淤泥。
偶尔还有人停留在它面前，俯下身从袖子里掏出肉饼，掰碎了放在地上。凉了，但还是香的。
喂它的人隔几日就来。毛毡也习惯了晒太阳之余走过大殿张望四周——总有几个熟悉的声音会叫住它。
“它的毛软乎乎的，就像条毡子，真暖。”
“毛毡过来！”他们每从大殿出来，就如释重负地呼唤毛毡，放下吃食。
“天威庄严，今日不犯错，已属幸事。“人抚摸着毛毡的脑袋，感慨又平安度过了一天，毛毡喵了一声当做回应。
人们来来往往。而毛毡只在乎今天是否放晴。
en:
Felt opens its eyes lazily and shifts its rump with obvious reluctance.

The east side of Chongde Hall's plaza is its favorite corner. In winter, it gets the warm afternoon sun there.
Before it knows it, the sun has slid to the other side. Felt follows the warmth and flops back down.

Every few days, this place turns lively for a while. When that happens, Felt hides in the shrubs and watches people in robes of different colors stream in and out.
Some footsteps are light, as if a wind could lift them skyward.
Others drag with heavy sighs, breath like silt settling in still water.

Sometimes someone stops in front of Felt, bends down, pulls out a meat cake from a sleeve, and crumbles it onto the ground.
It's cold, but it still smells good.

The person who feeds it comes every few days. And Felt has gotten used to wandering over after sunbathing to look around the hall.
A few familiar voices always call out.

"Its fur is so soft, like felt. So warm."
"Felt, come here!"

Each time they leave the hall, they call for Felt with a visible sense of relief and set food down.
"The imperial presence is daunting. Making it through today without a mistake is already a blessing."

A hand strokes Felt's head, grateful that another day has passed in one piece. Felt answers with a single meow.

People come and go.
Felt only cares whether the sky stays clear today.

zh:
史三水和蔡小辰翻过了一座雪山，来到一处幽深的洞口前。
蔡小辰神秘兮兮地说：“这可是我一个人发现的哦！听说凉州雪山里，有宝藏！”
史三水撇撇嘴：“我阿爷阿娘要是知道咱们跑这么远，会和你阿爷阿娘一起打断我们的腿！”
“怕什么！就老规矩，都说是我带头的！”蔡小辰边说边打开背包，掏出一堆七零八落的东西。史三水探头一看，什么火折子，毛毡子，小冰镐，一应俱全，色色俱备。最后，蔡小辰还不忘掏出个纸包丢给史三水。
“玛仁糖，上次你说爱吃，我央我阿娘多买了一份。”
史三水将纸包打开。玛仁糖受冷，变得邦邦硬。未等史三水开口，蔡小辰又把火折子分史三水一个。 “热着吃。”
火焰炙烤，玛仁糖的香气像涟漪一样扩散开。蔡小辰和史三水慢慢向洞中走去。
突然，前方的黑暗中传来一阵低吼。两个孩子立刻吓得不敢动弹。幽幽两盏灯火亮起，竟是那冬眠的熊罴被吵醒。
“跑！”蔡小辰眼疾手快，拉起还在发呆的史三水转身就逃。
史三水都要忘了自己是怎么一路回家的。她只记得，蔡小辰始终紧紧钳着自己的手，两个人尖叫，摔倒，爬起，浑身泥泞。但蔡小辰的手一直没有放开。

猎户在镇里四处告示，雪山上的熊罴惊醒，但未下山。他分明看到，那熊罴竟捧着几块玛仁糖吃得香甜。
而跪在屋子里的两个孩子，正被训斥地不敢抬头。
趁着阿爷喝口水的功夫，史三水悄咪咪抬起头，看到蔡小辰也歪着嘴角。他的鼻尖被冰碴磕破，浅浅地渗着血。
相识一笑，孩子再听不到责骂声，只剩下彼此眼中的烛火。
en:
Shi Sanshui and Cai Xiaochen crossed a snowy mountain and arrived before a deep cave entrance. 
Cai Xiaochen said mysteriously, "I found this alone! They say there's treasure in the Liangzhou snow mountains!" 
Shi Sanshui pouted. "If my parents knew we came this far, they'd join your parents in breaking our legs!" 
"Who's afraid! Same old rule—just say I led the way!" As he spoke, Cai Xiaochen opened his pack and pulled out a jumble of items. Shi Sanshui peeked: fire starters, felt pads, a small ice axe—everything needed, all accounted for. Finally, Cai Xiaochen didn't forget to toss a paper packet to Shi Sanshui. 
"Almond candy. You said you liked it last time, so I begged my mom to buy an extra portion." 
Shi Sanshui opened the packet. The candy had frozen rock-hard in the cold. Before she could speak, Cai Xiaochen handed her a fire starter. "Warm it up." 
The flame licked the candy, its fragrance spreading like ripples. Cai Xiaochen and Shi Sanshui slowly walked into the cave. 
Suddenly, a low growl came from the darkness ahead. The two children froze, terrified. Two faint lights glowed—it was a hibernating bear, awakened by the noise. 
"Run!" Quick-eyed, Cai Xiaochen grabbed the stunned Shi Sanshui and turned to flee. 
Shi Sanshui almost forgot how they got home. She only remembered Cai Xiaochen's hand tightly gripping hers the whole way. They screamed, fell, got up, covered in mud. But Cai Xiaochen's hand never let go. 

A hunter posted notices all over town: a bear on the mountain had been startled awake but hadn't come down. He clearly saw the bear happily eating pieces of almond candy. 
Meanwhile, the two children kneeling in the house, being scolded, didn't dare lift their heads. 
While her father paused for a sip of water, Shi Sanshui secretly glanced up and saw Cai Xiaochen also grinning, the corner of his mouth twitching. The tip of his nose was scraped by ice, bleeding slightly. 
They shared a knowing smile. The children no longer heard the scolding—only the candlelight reflected in each other's eyes.

zh:
金玉缘
新鲜鲈鱼，一尺长者为佳，以鸾刀片之，置于纸上稍加风干。
将姜、白梅、橘皮、栗子、甘草捣为末，再放入粳米、蒜，碾捣成泥，而后下醋解之，以山桃花瓣饰之。

醉别离
取瓯越蝤蛑，取蟹黄为金，取蟹肉为银，蟹肉和蟹黄相间铺于面皮之上，经绍酒醉蒸后一切为二，置于盘中南北，配圆兴山坞桂花。

两相思
将湿糯米粉打散，木桶中分别铺红豆与莲子心，以旺火沸水蒸制至软糯。将蒸熟的糯米团趁热倒入石臼中，反复捶打至糕团紧实绵密，将其压制成长方条状。

归乡客

相拌而食，相伴而餐。
en:
Golden Jade
Choose a fresh bass, ideally about one foot long. Slice it thinly with a fine knife, then lay the slices on paper to air-dry briefly.
Grind ginger, white plum, orange peel, chestnut, and licorice to a powder. Add short-grain rice and garlic, then pound into a paste. Loosen with vinegar and garnish with wild peach petals.

Drunken Parting
Take a fresh Ou-Yue mud crab and separate the golden roe from the pearly white meat. Layer the two alternately over a dough wrapper, then steam with Shaoxing wine. Cut the finished dish in half and arrange the two pieces at opposite ends of the plate. Finish with osmanthus from the Yuanxing hills.

Mutual Longing
Break up the damp glutinous rice flour. Arrange red beans and lotus seed hearts separately in a wooden barrel, then steam over high heat until soft and sticky. Transfer the hot rice dough to a stone mortar and pound until smooth and firm. Shape into long rectangular bars.

Traveler's Tears
A plate of Jiande pickled greens, a bowl of rice porridge, and a pot of warm wine.
Simple things, best enjoyed together, with someone beside you.

zh: 1979年出土于敦煌马圈湾汉代烽燧遗址。汉代出现了以相马立名天下的相马名家黄直、陈君夫，并有相马专著的问世。相马术在汉代已是一种专门技艺，甘肃敦煌马圈湾出土的这枚简牍就是关于相马方法的记载。“伯乐相马自有形”指伯乐根据马的形体相马之优劣。河西汉塞发现《相马经》残简从一个侧面说明了马在汉代人的生产、生活和军事活动中具有重要地位。
en: Discovered in 1979 at the Dunhuang Maquanwan Han Beacon Tower Site, this bamboo slip records ancient methods for evaluating horses. By the Han era, horse appraisal had become a highly specialized and respected craft. Master appraisers like Huang Zhi and Chen Junfu made names for themselves across the empire, and dedicated treatises on the subject began to circulate. The phrase "Bole judges a steed by its form" refers to the legendary expert's method of determining a horse's worth based on its physical build. Finding fragments of the Horse Appraisal Manual at these remote frontier garrisons in the Hexi Han Frontier highlights a crucial historical truth: horses were absolutely vital to the agriculture, daily life, and military campaigns of the Han people.

zh:
王大犬决定离家的那天，阿婆的头风疾正犯得厉害。
多年过去，王大犬早已出落地一表人才。这样的才俊，自是不甘囿于穷困的家乡。
阿婆歪在榻上，纵使头晕目眩，也拉着王大犬手，近乎哀求。
“且等等，我给你蒸屉馍馍。”

这也是这么多年第一次，王大犬在一边看着阿婆蒸馍馍。
磨好的麦粉要再过一遍筛——毕竟风大，容易掺进沙子。用澄清的井水细细和面，再从罐子里揪一块老面做引子揉在一起。
用透气的竹篾子遮着发面，再从屋里取一块肥油细细切碎，丢在外面吹风。
阿婆的嘴也没闲着。“记得按时吃饭，想吃啥吃啥。”“记得按时穿衣服。不够的就往家里寄信。”“在外面别惹事，看着不对就跑”……
絮絮叨叨，零零碎碎。面发好了，肥油也干了大半。
阿婆一边费劲地喘着气儿揉着面，一边支使王大犬把馍馍码到笼屉里。
豆大的汗水淅淅沥沥跌在面板上。王大犬第一次发现，阿婆老了。
记忆里那如山峦一般高大的身躯，不过也才到自己的胸口。她的面容也渐渐干瘪，不复昔年。
阿婆把柴禾堆到灶里，再把肥油碎码上。添水，引火，起灶，肥油在火中噼啪作响。空气中的麦香和肉香混合，蒸汽氤氲了阿婆的眸子。
“好孩子，记得想阿婆。”
en:
The day Wang Daquan decided to leave home, Grandma's chronic headaches were acting up terribly. 
Many years had passed. Wang Daquan had grown into a fine young man. Such talent naturally chafed against the confines of his impoverished hometown. 
Grandma lay slumped on the bed, dizzy and faint, yet she clung to Wang Daquan's hand, her plea almost a whisper. 
"Just wait... let me steam a tray of buns for you." 

For the first time in all these years, Wang Daquan stayed to watch Grandma make the buns. 
The milled wheat flour needed sifting again—the wind was strong, and sand got in too easily. She mixed it slowly with clear well water, then pinched off a piece of old dough from the jar to use as starter, kneading it all together. 
The dough was left to rise under a breathable bamboo cover. She took a piece of fat from the house, chopped it finely, and set it outside to dry in the wind. 
Grandma's mouth didn't rest either. "Remember to eat on time, eat whatever you want." "Remember to dress warmly. If you need anything, write home." "Don't stir up trouble outside. If something looks wrong, just run"... 
Bits and pieces, murmured over and over. The dough rose; the fat dried halfway. 
Panting with effort, Grandma kneaded the dough while directing Wang Daquan to arrange the buns in the steamer. 
Sweat the size of beans pattered onto the board. For the first time, Wang Daquan realized: Grandma had aged. 
The towering figure from his memory now only reached his chest. Her face had grown gaunt, no longer what it once was. 
Grandma stacked firewood in the stove, then scattered the chopped fat over it. She added water, lit the fire, and started the stove. The fat crackled in the flames. The scent of wheat and meat mingled in the air, and steam clouded Grandma's eyes. 
"Good child... remember to think of your grandma."

Today I happened upon a group holding a literary gathering in a pavilion. Any time there's a literary gathering, you can be sure they forgot to invite me, so of course I cheerfully went right in.
They were taking turns composing verse, and literary inspiration was pouring out of me. I answered each line on the spot. One fellow recited, "Willows green and blossoms red stir the sorrows of spring," and I immediately replied, "Flies buzz and grass goes long, stew the meat and bring it on!"
After a few rounds, the whole table sat there in stunned silence. It seems my reputation as a once-in-a-generation literary giant can no longer be hidden. Ahem. If any invitations to literary gatherings arrive at your place, do not decline them for me. I will certainly attend.

对于小妖这人，外人态度不一。
有人爱她，因她实在美丽；也有人恨她，因她太过多情；而更多的人，对她又爱又恨，简直不知该如何是好。
“不知该如何是好？那与我何干？”小厮带回外界的蜚语时，于小妖正在镜前梳妆。闻言她浅浅一笑，手下却未停。但见一勾一抹间，眉似远山，眼如秋波，煞是勾人心魄。而后她款款起身，穿过一众目光，聘婷离去。

揣测，蜚语，探究……对于小妖而言，向来不过尔尔。她真正在乎的，只有一件事——她想要理清，所谓情爱，到底是何物。
那物什定是什么宝物。不然，怎能叫她的母亲丢下年幼的女儿，抛下拥有的一切，跑去换了脸，还丢了命？
在她大些的时候，她带着这个疑惑，找到了那让母亲魂牵梦绕的男人。但她很失望。
那个男人粗鄙、无趣。倒于血泊之中的时候，那浑身上下，更是揪不出一寸好来。
所以情爱二字，定是个世间的诅咒，能让人失了智，丢了自己。

于是于小妖开始四处寻情。最初，她从不以真面目示人。她承了她母亲的一双巧手，寥寥几笔，便可化作世上的任何人。她扮演那些人的爱人，去听他们的海誓山盟，去观他们的浓情蜜意。但很快，她就开始厌倦。因她发现无论是何种人，陷于情爱时，都变得愚钝，蠢得无甚区别。再后来，她发现了旁人看她时眼中的流转。于是她褪下伪装，笑脸迎去。但很快，她再次开始厌倦。因她发现情爱也不过如此，不堪一击，浅薄又无力。

最后……最后她就成了而今这模样。偶尔示好，但也止步于示好；时常作乐，但从不贪欢。她察人之情态，揣人之心怀，还在试图理清，何为情爱。
还有的时候，她对镜贴妆，对闻讯而来的痴男怨女扬起笑颜，而后说起自己这些年的故事。
她想让他们明白，此间浩瀚，而爱浅薄，若因而丢了心，弃了命，实在可惜哪。
en:
Opinions about Yu Xiaoyao are as divided as the wind. 
Some adore her for her stunning beauty, others loathe her for her perceived "fickleness." But most found themselves torn between the two, utterly at a loss.
"At a loss? What concern is that of mine?" When a pageboy relayed the gossip, Yu Xiaoyao was applying makeup before a mirror. A faint smile touched her lips, but her hand never faltered, each stroke precise, until her eyes gleamed like autumn rivers, her brows arched like distant mountains, a vision to steal any heart. 
Then she rose, gliding past the stares, leaving only perfume and longing in her wake.

Rumors, speculation, prying eyes... these meant nothing to her. Only one question truly mattered: What, exactly, was this thing called love?
It must be something precious. Why else would her mother abandon her young daughter, cast aside everything, even change her face, only to die for it?
Older now, she sought out the man who had haunted her mother's dreams. And was sorely disappointed.
The man was coarse, dull. As he lay bleeding out, she could find no redeeming quality in him.
Love wasn't treasure. It was a curse. One that robbed people of a sense and self.

So Yu Xiaoyao began a quest to study love. At first, she never showed her true face. Blessed with her mother's talent for disguise, she could mimic anyone with a few brushstrokes. She posed as lovers, listening to their vows, observing their passion, only to grow bored. All lovers become fools in the end, she realized, their idiocy indistinguishable across class and status. Later, noticing the hunger in men's eyes when they looked at her, she dropped her masks and smiled openly, only to grow bored again. Love, she concluded, was fragile, shallow, and powerless.

Now... now she was as you saw her. Offering warmth, but never devotion, delighting in games, but never losing herself. She studied hearts, parsed yearnings, still searching for an answer.
Sometimes, as she paints her face or smiles at lovesick admirers, she shares stories of her journey.
She wants them to understand that the world is vast, but love is fleeting, so do not lose your soul for it.

zh:
伊刀承认，他终日打鹰，没想到有一日被家雀啄了眼。
也许是在酒窖里的合作愉快，让他对这小崽子有了错误的信赖。
直到又被那狡猾的崽子坑了一把，狼狈不堪地被寒香寻救下。
伊刀想要长叹一声——
哼，不跟毛都没长齐的小崽子计较。
他没有忘记自己的来意，没有忘记此行是为了一个承诺——重逾千金。
只是江湖寥落，故友飘零。
将消息带给寒香寻的时候，看到她一瞬间的失魂，伊刀有些不自在。
他向来不擅长应付这些场面，也不愿看被留下之人的神情。
那眉梢眼底里，有些东西，叫人心头发麻。
江湖，这该死的江湖！

“我一直想到江湖上去看看。”
小崽子说。
伊刀想嘲笑，哈，你也想去江湖？
算了吧，你这口伶牙俐齿，一张嘴指不定还能得罪多少人。
江湖上的人，可不都像老子这么好脾气，被得罪狠了，还能饶你一命……
可他又想，很像。这小崽子，很像他。
这神仙渡，是好。可是太小了，小到经不起雏鸟化为鹏的第一次振翅。
留不住，那鹏鸟哪怕翅膀尚软，也会跌跌撞撞地起飞，一次次尝试着飞出巢穴。
哪怕外面便是万丈深渊，跌下去粉身碎骨。
罢了罢了，伊刀想着。
“走，老子带你去开封！”
有他伊刀一天在，定不会让这小崽子跌下去，摔得粉碎。
en:
Yi Dao had to admit, he'd spent his whole life hunting hawks, but never thought he'd get pecked in the eye by a sparrow. Maybe it was because they'd worked so well together in that wine cellar that he'd mistakenly started to trust the little brat. Until that sly kid tricked him again, leaving him in a sorry state, only to be rescued by Han Xiangxun herself. Yi Dao wanted to let out a long sigh—Forget it. No point holding a grudge against a snot-nosed brat.
He hadn't forgotten his true purpose, hadn't forgotten the promise he came for—a promise worth more than gold. But the Jianghu had grown desolate, old friends scattered to the wind. When he delivered the news to Han Xiangxun and saw that fleeting emptiness in her eyes, Yi Dao felt uneasy. He was never good at handling such moments, and never wanted to see the faces of those left behind. There was something in her eyes, in her expression, that made his heart go numb. Jianghu, damn this wretched jianghu!

"I've always wanted to see what the Jianghu outside is like," the kid said. Yi Dao almost laughed. You? Want to go into the Jianghu? Please. With that sharp tongue of yours, who knows how many people you'd offend just by talking? People out there aren't as easygoing as me; push them too far and they won't let you off so easily... But then, he thought, the kid was very much like himself.
Heaven's Pier was a good place, but it was too small, too fragile to withstand a fledgling's first attempt to soar like a roc. You can't keep it in; even if the wings are still soft, that young bird will stumble and try to fly, again and again, out of the nest—even if outside is a bottomless abyss, and falling means being smashed to pieces.
Forget it, Yi Dao thought. "Come on, I'll take you to Kaifeng!" As long as Yi Dao was around, he'd never let that kid fall and shatter to pieces.

zh:
山外来的游侠：
都说跟着妙妙喵的寻龙尺走，就能找着真正的宝贝。可别说这寻龙尺的动静了，那妙妙喵也总是来无影去无踪，我足足翘了半个月的课，这才寻到了它的踪迹。可我们几个同门跟着它爬了半天的山，宝藏到没找着，只见着了熟睡的游侠。
难不成那宝贝就在游侠身上？还是说……游侠就是妙妙喵要找的宝贝？
游侠迟迟不醒，妙妙喵也迟迟不离。原本打算去妙妙庙参拜的同道们，渐渐都寻到这儿来，奉上书卷，祈求学业顺遂，考校通过。时间长了，连山里的猴子也仿着弟子们，将野果衔来此地。难道它们也有课业之忧？还是说，它们也在替墨门弟子祈愿？
不知是妙妙喵显灵，还是猴儿们诚心，抑或是游侠所处果真为智慧流转之地，来此参拜过的弟子，考校果然有所进益！同道们便凑了些墨筹，给妙妙喵备了点小鱼干，给猴子们带了碧水云涛的桃子，也给游侠附了份谢礼。
山物简陋，不成敬意，与游侠这番机缘，墨门弟子定当时常感念！
en:
Dear Wanderer,
They say Meow Meow's Dragonfinder will lead you to the real treasure. Yet the rod remains silent, and Meow Meow is like a ghost without a trace. I skipped class for a full half month before I finally found its trail. A few of us from the sect followed it up the mountain for ages, but instead of treasure, all we found was you, fast asleep.
Could the treasure be on you? Or perhaps... Could you be the treasure Meow Meow was looking for?
As you remained in your deep slumber, Meow Meow wouldn't leave. Soon, disciples bound for Meow Meow Temple found their way here instead, offering scrolls and praying for smooth studies and successful exams. After a while, even the mountain monkeys started following suit, carrying wild fruit over in their mouths. Do monkeys worry about homework too? Or were they praying on behalf of us Mohist disciples?
Whether it was Meow Meow's grace, the monkeys' sincerity, or the fact that your resting place is a confluence of wisdom, those who came to pay their respects have indeed seen their marks flourish! Thus, we chipped in some Mohist Tallies to get dried fish for Meow Meow, peaches from Jadestream Valley for the monkeys, and a small thank-you gift for you as well.

It's not much, just a few humble mountain offerings, but we Mohist disciples will always be grateful for this strange little stroke of fate that brought us to you!

zh:
余行至思危阁，渐闻水声潺潺，林木愈深。路尽处，忽见一峰突起，孤绝如剑，直插云霄。四周沧海环绕，烟波浩渺，望之若海上仙山。此即金声岭也。
岭上石楼巍然，砖石垒之，与山体浑然天成，历经风雨而愈显苍劲。其下广约数丈，内设垂梯而上。爬至楼顶，但见碧波万顷，鸥鸟低翔，远帆如豆，隐现天际。顶悬木铎，每每击之，声如雷震，滚滚而落，弥漫四野。风起时，钟声与松涛相和，或沉或昂，恍若天地同鸣。
岭侧有栈道悬空，依危崖而凿。工匠先于岩壁凿孔，架木为梁，上铺厚板，盘旋而上。临此地者，但见脚下沧波万里，云海翻涌，有凛凛之风自足下起，不觉股栗。
余登上绝顶，临风而立，四望空阔，天地无垠。远处海天一色，苍茫难辨；近处松涛阵阵，随风摆之。钟楼巍然立于身后，静默如磐石。此时但觉胸中积郁一洗而空，尘世扰攘皆不可闻。
金声一振，非止传于百里，更入人心。天下向学之士，闻此钟声，当知此山有铎，此铎有道。千年之下，钟声不绝，道脉亦不绝矣。
en:
As I walked toward Vigilance Pavilion, the sound of flowing water grew louder, and the forest deepened. At the road's end, a solitary peak suddenly rose before me, sharp and isolated like a sword piercing the heavens. Surrounded by boundless sea and misty waves, it looked like an immortal mountain rising from the ocean. This was Goldentone Ridge.
Atop the ridge stood a towering stone tower, built of brick and stone, blending seamlessly with the mountain itself, growing ever more rugged through wind and rain. Below it stretched a broad courtyard several arm-spans wide, with a hanging ladder leading up. Climbing to the tower's summit, one beheld endless blue waves, gulls skimming low, distant sails like tiny beans fading in and out along the horizon. A wooden bell hung at the peak. Each strike rang out like thunder, rolling across the land. When the wind rose, the bell's tone mingled with the roar of the pines, rising and falling as though heaven and earth resonated together.
Beside the ridge, a plank road hung suspended, carved into the sheer cliff face. Artisans first drilled holes into the rock, then set wooden beams across, laying thick planks atop them, winding upward. Standing here, one saw endless blue waves far below, clouds churning like a sea, a chilling wind rising from beneath one's feet, enough to make the legs tremble.
Reaching the very summit, I stood facing the wind, gazing out at the boundless expanse of heaven and earth. In the distance, sea and sky blurred into one, vast and indistinct; nearby, the pines rustled in waves, swaying with the breeze. The bell tower stood firm behind me, silent as a boulder. In that moment, all the pent-up cares in my chest seemed washed away, and the clamor of the mortal world fell utterly silent.
The tolling of Goldentone carries not merely a hundred miles, but straight into the human heart. Scholars throughout the land, upon hearing this bell, shall know that this mountain holds a bell, and this bell holds the Way. A thousand years hence, the bell's toll shall not cease, nor shall the lineage of the Way.

zh:
当日仓卒，未遑深虑，今之视昔……
城坠一劫，吾有三错。
一错，身在迷阵，不能与诸位同门……同蹈此难……
况罔论天意人谋……定早有征兆……独耽问诛之事……先是延请长老证之……
后……赴约……诸事种种，乃致竟未觉察……
二错，失约于至亲……害燕隼遭得此劫……
仅守燕一日，又未能候其醒转，不辞而别……
两孩儿至慧，安遭此厄？城中诸同门，更又何辜……
三错，闻城中复灼，即刻奔往，未留片语……
至天衍室方知，那 ███ 竟接于算阵枢机……虽不知谁以铸铁匣封之……然挽得一时，仍复灼意沸天……
算阵百年推演，崩颓在即……更有爆燃毁山之险……唯以身作桥……以心脉引炁……导转……算阵机枢……
……
切盼汝见此信时……吾已身竭功成……
百代之功，终未枉费……
算阵可再启之……飞天之志……可盼……
en:
In those hurried days, there was no time for deeper thought. Looking back now...
In the calamity of the falling city, I made three grave mistakes.
First: I was trapped inside the maze array and could not face this disaster alongside my fellow disciples...
Never mind whether it was Heaven's will or man's design... there must have been signs long before... yet I fixated only on the matter of accusation and punishment... first inviting the elders to bear witness...
Then... there was that appointment... one thing after another... and in the end I noticed nothing...
Second: I broke faith with those dearest to me... and brought this calamity upon Swallow and Falcon...
I kept watch by Swallow's side for only a single day, then left before he woke, without a word...
Those two children are so clever. How could they have met such a fate? And what wrong had all our fellow disciples in the city ever done...
Third: when I heard the city had caught fire again, I rushed there at once and left not a single word behind...
Only when I reached the Chamber of Derivation did I learn that ███ had in fact been connected to the array's central workings... I still do not know who sealed it inside an iron casing... though it bought us a little time, the blaze soon surged skyward again...
After a hundred years of calculation and projection, the array stood on the brink of collapse... worse still, there was the danger of an explosion that could destroy the mountain... There was no choice but to use my own body as a bridge... to guide qi through my inner meridian... and redirect... the array's central mechanism...
...
I can only hope that by the time you read this letter... I will already have spent myself utterly, and the work will be complete...
Then the labor of generations will not have been wasted after all...
The calculation array may yet be set in motion again... and the dream of flight... may yet live on...

zh:
【庄公第三】

元年，春，王正月。
继弒君不言即位，正也。继弒君不言即位之为正，何也？曰先君不以其道终，则子不忍即位也。
○三月，夫人孙于齐。
孙之为言犹逊也，讳奔也。接练时，录母之变，始人之也。不言氏姓，贬之也。人之于天也，以道受命；于人也，以言受命。不若于道者，天绝之也；不若于言者，人绝之也。臣子大受命。
○夏，单伯逆王姬。
单伯者何？吾大夫之命乎天子者也。命大夫，故不名也。其不言如何也？其义不可受于京师也。其义不可受于京师何也？曰躬君弒于齐，使之主婚，与齐为礼，其义固不可受也。
○秋，筑王姬之馆于外。
筑，礼也。于外，非礼也。筑之为礼何也？主王姬者，必自公门出。于庙则已尊，于寝则已卑。为之筑，节矣。筑之外，变之正也。筑之外变之为正何也？仇仇之人，非所以接婚姻也。衰麻非所以接弁冕也。其不言齐侯之来逆何也？不使齐侯得与吾为礼也。
○冬，十月，乙亥，陈侯林卒。
诸侯日卒，正也。
○王使荣叔来锡桓公命。
礼有受命，无来锡命。锡命，非正也。生服之，死行之，礼也。生不服，死追锡之，不正甚矣。
○王姬归于齐。
为之中者归之也。
○齐师迁纪、郱、鄑、郚。
郱、鄑、郚，国也。或曰：迁纪于郱、鄑、郚。

二年，春，王二月，葬陈庄公。
○夏，公子庆父帅师伐于余丘。
国而曰伐。于余丘，邾之邑也。其曰伐何也？公子贵矣，师重矣，而敌人之邑，公子病矣。病公子，所以讥乎公也。其一曰，君在而重之也。
○秋，七月，齐王姬卒。
为之主者，卒之也。
○冬，十有二月，夫人姜氏会齐侯于禚。
妇人既嫁，不踰竟。踰竟，非正也。妇人不言会，言会，非正也。
○乙酉，宋公冯卒。

……
en:
【Duke Zhuang, Part Three】

First Year, Spring, the King's First Month.
Not announcing the succession after the death of a murdered ruler is proper. Why is not announcing the succession after the death of a murdered ruler considered proper? It is said: when the former ruler did not meet his end in accordance with the Way, the son cannot bear to assume the throne.
○Third Month, the Lady retreated to Qi.
"Retreated" is a euphemism for fleeing, concealing the act of escape. At the time of the mourning rites, the change in the mother's status was recorded, marking the beginning of her recognition as a person. Not mentioning her surname and clan is a reproach of her. In relation to Heaven, one receives the mandate through the Way; in relation to others, one receives the mandate through words. Those who do not conform to the Way are cut off by Heaven; those who do not conform to words are cut off by others. Ministers and sons greatly receive the mandate.
○Summer, Shan Bo went to meet the King's daughter.
Who is Shan Bo? He is one of our ministers appointed by the Emperor. As an appointed minister, his name is not mentioned. Why is it not said that he went to meet her? Because according to propriety, it could not be done in the capital. Why could it not be done in the capital according to propriety? It is said: since the ruler himself was murdered in Qi, having him preside over the marriage and observe rites with Qi would fundamentally violate propriety.
○Autumn, a pavilion for the King's daughter was built outside the city.
Building it was proper. Building it outside was improper. Why was building it considered proper? The one hosting the King's daughter must depart through the public gate. In the ancestral temple it would be too venerable; in the private chambers it would be too lowly. Building a pavilion for her was a measure of moderation. Building it outside was a correction of the irregularity. Why was building it outside considered a correction? Those who are enemies are not fit to conduct marriage rites. Mourning garments are not fit to accompany ceremonial caps. Why is it not mentioned that the Marquis of Qi came to meet her? It is to prevent the Marquis of Qi from participating in rites with us.
○Winter, Tenth Month, on the day Yihai, Marquis Lin of Chen died.
Recording the day of a feudal lord's death is proper.
○The King sent Rong Shu to come and bestow posthumous orders on Duke Huan.
According to rites, there is receiving orders, but no coming to bestow orders. Bestowing orders is improper. Serving them in life and implementing them in death is proper. Not serving them in life but pursuing their bestowal after death is greatly improper.
○The King's daughter returned to Qi.
She who was hosted by us returned to her own state.
○The Qi army relocated Ji, Ping, Zin, and Wu.
Ping, Zin, and Wu were states. Some say: Ji was relocated to Ping, Zin, and Wu.

Second Year, Spring, the King's Second Month, burial of Duke Zhuang of Chen.
○Summer, Prince Qingfu led troops to attack Yu Yuqiu.
For a state, it is called "attacking." Yu Yuqiu is a city of Zhu. Why is it called "attacking"? The prince is noble, the army is weighty, yet attacking a city of the enemy makes the prince's task burdensome. Making the prince's task burdensome is a way to criticize the duke. Another interpretation says: because the ruler was present, the matter was treated with gravity.
○Autumn, Seventh Month, the King's daughter of Qi died.
She who was hosted by us had her death recorded.
○Winter, Twelfth Month, Lady Jiang of the wife met the Marquis of Qi at Zhuo.
A married woman should not cross the border. Crossing the border is improper. For a woman, meetings are not spoken of; speaking of a meeting is improper.
○On the day Yiyou, Duke Feng of Song died.

万无忧从来就不喜欢自己的名字。

无忧，无忧……二十岁的万无忧躺在屋顶，嘴上嚼着松子，心里嚼着自己的名字。
没有忧愁是什么样的感觉呢？她就算是逃了工，内心也总是愁着，愁着一会回去爹娘会不会又唉声叹气，愁着自己会不会爹爹一样，一辈子就做个抡锤子的匠人。
月亮沉到西边的山下，无忧起身拍拍屁股准备回家。晚风凉凉，把一缕陌生的香气卷进无忧鼻中。
那香气像是爹爹起炉时跳窜的火星子，像夏夜阿娘哼着歌给她编的草扇子。那香气勾得人忘记了烦恼，忘记了年岁，好像远方的山变得很高很高，她是花间歇息的小瓢虫；又好像她自己变得很大很大，一伸手，把月亮从山的那边提回了天上。
以为仓库遭了贼的狄娟、狄福提着灯笼，看到的就是这样一副情景——
女孩枕着一坛中山松醪酒，抱着一坛被她喝光的千年醉，腿上还压着一杠子酒，四仰八叉地躺在仓库里呼呼大睡。
“咱都还没开业，怎么就醉倒了一个？”
“嘘，别把她吵醒了。看那样子，一定是做了个没有烦恼的好梦……”
en:
Wan Wuyou doesn't like her name at all.
It sounded like it belonged to a young lady behind embroidered screens in Kaifeng, or a wandering Daoist girl drifting beyond the mountains, anyone but her. Certainly not a dust-streaked girl who'd grown up in the shadowy folds of Mirkvale.
Wuyou, means "no worries" in Chinese... At twenty, she lay flat on a rooftop, cracking pine nuts between her teeth and chewing over those two words in her head. What did "no worries" even feel like? Even when she skipped work to steal a bit of peace, her heart stayed busy, worrying whether her parents would sigh again when she got home, worrying whether she'd end up like her father, hammer in hand, stuck in the same trade for life.
When the moon slid behind the western hills, Wuyou brushed off the dust and climbed down. The night breeze was cool, carrying with it a thread of unfamiliar scent.
It smelled like sparks leaping from her father's forge. Like summer nights when her mother hummed softly while weaving grass fans. The scent tugged at her until worries slipped loose, time blurred... The distant mountains seemed impossibly tall, and she was a ladybug resting among flowers. She felt herself becoming enormous, certain that if she reached out, she could lift the moon back into the sky.
Di Juan and Di Fu came running with lanterns, thinking thieves had broken into the storeroom. What they found instead was...
A girl sprawled on the floor, head pillowed on a jar of Zhongshan Pine Brew, clutching an empty cask marked Sweet Slumber, another jug pinned under her legs, sleeping like the dead.
"We haven't even opened yet. How did someone already get drunk?"
"Hush—Look at her. She must be having a dream with no worries at all..."

zh:
游侠，见字如面。
前些时日，老朽随府尹大人巡查蒙学，见学堂里的娃娃们一个个正襟危坐，埋首书卷，连我等走近了都未曾察觉。
老朽心下好奇，是何等妙文，能让这些上蹿下跳的娃娃们如此专心？一问才知，他们手中所读，竟是你前些时日所赠。
老朽又问，这些书好在何处？娃娃们七嘴八舌，老朽这才知道，原来你竟为每个孩子都择了不同的书，实在是费心了。而听闻老朽与你相熟，他们都央着我，定要代他们向你道声谢。
只是，真要问他们想说什么，这群小家伙却面露羞赧，讷讷而止了。最后，老朽想了个法子，让他们把想说的话都诉诸笔端，一并封在信里了。至于写了什么，老朽绝未偷看！
对了，娃娃们还托我转交几幅画作，说是读了书卷后的有感而发。他们都说，游侠你是他们见过最有眼光的人，定能欣赏他们的大作。
哈哈，看来往后若再有与孩子们打交道的差事，找游侠准是没错了。
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/68ce413fe93aa962b2a631970eWhtJri06' size='1446*1052' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>
<IMAGE id='im2' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/68ce4147b9031a57f31d7fee6Ypeg61O06' size='1965*2469' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>
en:
Dear Wanderer,

The other day, I accompanied the Prefect on an inspection of the village school. The children sat straight at their desks, noses buried in scrolls, so absorbed they didn't even notice us draw near.
Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

zh:
长兴四年，元月初五
闻冯公九经将成，余心甚悦，乃以雕版之术为贺。不意酒酣耳热之际，冯道老叟竟携余观其文津馆十相弟子，扬言“皆国器也”。
噫！厚颜何至此哉？吾虽平日尝讥门下三子不肖，岂真以为朽木之材耶？
首徒万师，幼立治水之志。四岁入墨门，八岁尽通水工之机巧，十岁即能指摘长老疏漏。倘假以岁月，平定水患，必当青史留名。
次徒启蛰，敏而寡言，温润好学。诸般机关尽得其妙，百家典册皆纳于胸。假以时日，待其融汇百家，纵尔文津群彦，何者能出其右。
三徒祁青，尚义任侠，四岁筑基，五岁执剑，六岁通三门剑术，八岁可搏虎豹，若使文津习武，定当仗剑叩馆，与诸生论技。
文津十相，不过先饮数年墨耳！老叟且待，不日吾三子必声震寰宇。届时当令彼等拜门，薅尔苍髯！
en:
5th Day of the First Month, fourth year of Changxing
Hearing that Master Feng's Nine Classics were nearly complete, I was greatly pleased, and so offered woodblock printing as my congratulations. Who would have thought that, with the wine barely warm in us, that old fellow Feng Dao would drag me off to behold the ten "Sages" of his Inkbound Order, loudly declaring, "All are vessels of state."
Ha. How can a man be so shameless? I may at times scold the three disciples under my roof for being unworthy, but do I truly take them for mere rotten wood?
My first disciple, Wanshi, set his heart on taming the waters while still a child. He entered Mohist Hill at four, had mastered the mechanisms of waterworks by eight, and by ten could already point out the oversights of elder masters. Give him a few more years, and when he brings flood and torrent to heel, his name will surely be written in the histories.
My second disciple, Qizhe, is keen of mind and sparing of speech, gentle in temper and eager to learn. He has grasped the subtleties of every kind of mechanism, and carries within him the learning of a hundred schools. Given time, once he has truly fused them into one, then among all the bright talents of the Inkbound Order, who could stand above him?
My third disciple, Qi Halcyon, is righteous by nature and chivalrous in spirit. At four she laid her foundations, at five she took up the sword, at six she had mastered the sword arts of three schools, and by eight she could wrestle tiger and leopard alike. If the Inkbound Order ever turned its hand to martial training, she would surely stride to their gate with sword in hand and challenge their disciples to test their skill.
Those ten "Sages" of the Inkbound Order have merely had a few years' head start in drinking the ink of learning. Let that old fellow wait and see. Before long, my three disciples will make their names known under Heaven. And when that day comes, I shall send them to his gate to tug at that grey beard of his.

zh:
一日贺津前往野外采摘羌簧花。木箭破空之声正当面门，她就地伏下，躲过此等杀身之祸。
不远处跑来一人，看装束似是猎户。贺津把木箭从沙上拔出，递给此人。
猎户被贺津的眼神吓了一跳，嗫嚅道：“额觉着四周有狼，才发了箭哩。”

“那，你看我像狼么？”
“这么好一个女子，怎么会是狼哩。”
“多谢。你下回看准了再放箭。”
“额晓得！额也是糊涂了，狼都是一群群地出没，怎么可能只有一匹……”

话音未落，猎户忽地打了个寒颤。他以手搭弓，战战兢兢地转身，却见不远处有一男子，正牢牢盯着自己，缓步而来。
原来另一匹狼此时才姗姗来迟！
猎户只来得及转头与贺津简单道别，便仓皇逃跑了。

风又起了。感知到身后的压力已然消弭，猎户回头望了望。
两个人影在风沙中渐渐模糊、晕开，凝结成了遥远的一点，再不可寻。
en:
One day, He Jin went into the wild to pick Qianghuang flowers. The sound of a wooden arrow cutting through the air rushed toward her face. She dropped to the ground immediately, escaping the fatal blow. 
A man ran over from not far away, dressed like a hunter. He Jin pulled the wooden arrow out of the sand and handed it to him. 
Startled by He Jin's gaze, the hunter mumbled: "I thought there were wolves around, so I shot the arrow." 

"Then, do I look like a wolf?" 
"Such a fine lady, how could you be a wolf?" 
"Thank you. Next time, see carefully before you shoot." 
"I know! I was muddled. Wolves always come in packs, how could there be just one…" 

Before he finished speaking, the hunter suddenly shuddered. He drew his bow with trembling hands and turned around, only to see a man not far away staring firmly at him, walking slowly closer. 
So the other wolf had arrived late! 
The hunter barely had time to glance back and say a hasty farewell to He Jin before fleeing in panic. 

The wind picked up again. Feeling the threat behind him had disappeared, the hunter looked back. 
The two figures gradually blurred and faded in the wind and sand, shrinking into a distant dot, never to be found again.

zh:
张万师从不喜饮酒。
带教青、鸦二人时，规矩不多，不能饮酒便是一条。饮酒伤人神觉，做工便易生偏差，由此虚费良材，如造杀业。
但出山再回后，张万师却化作了酒疯子。
每一闭眼，入耳便是那些嚎哭之声，入眼便是那些泥泞枯黄的脸。
“我救不了你们，我救不了你们……”
他已尽了全力。他知道，一坛一坛灌下那些酒不过是根稻草，最后的稻草。稻草亦果然崩断，但他仍止不住会想：
若当日他真的喝完了，是不是便真能得到那理河修堤之权，一切会不会不一样？但死的人不会复生，洪涛下次还会肆意奔涌……
原来世上真有无论如何也做不到的事，原来天才之名从来是自居，原来竟是百无一用！
他的手剧烈颤抖着，又掂起了酒坛。
想了亦疯，不想亦疯。百无一用，此便归途！
且醉死在这无忧无愁——死无葬身之地吧！
en:
Zhang Wanshi never cared for wine. When teaching Halcyon and Crane, he kept few rules, but abstaining from wine was one of them. Wine dulled the mind and the senses, and a single lapse could ruin a piece of fine work, wasting precious materials, which is no different from committing a sin.

But after returning from beyond the peaks, Zhang Wanshi became a broken drunkard. Whenever he closed his eyes, his ears filled with the sound of wailing. Before him rose a sea of faces, hollow, mud-caked, and drained of all color.
"I couldn't save you. I couldn't save any of you."

He had given everything he had. He knew well enough that drowning himself in jar after jar of wine was nothing more than clutching at the last fraying straw. That straw had long since snapped, and yet he could not stop asking himself: if he had truly drained every last drop that day, would they have given him the authority to harness the river and shore up the dikes? Would any of it have been different?
But the dead do not come back, and the floodwaters would rage again without mercy.

So there truly are things beyond the reach of human hands. "Genius" was a title he had bestowed upon himself. In the end, it amounted to nothing at all.

His hands trembled violently as he reached for the wine jar once more. To remember is madness. To forget, madness still. Good for nothing. Then let this be my end. Let me drown here in oblivion, and perish with not even a grave to bear my name.

zh:
郎君钱多：

是我，云娘。近来天渐寒了，院子里积起了雪，也不知比起北边的是厚了还是薄了。爹娘颇照顾我，却也日日念叨你，不知你几时能回来。

外头辛苦，天凉了千万记得添衣、多吃热食，别委屈自己。他们都说北边乱，我也不知究竟乱成了什么样子，你只消记得：你师父从不指望谁替他报仇，只愿你们师兄弟俩都好好儿的。我也是这般想的。如此，替我向金重哥也带声好。

你走后不久，我便发现自己有喜了。你瞧，咱们就快有自己的孩子了。这几夜睡觉时，总觉得腹中的孩子在动。郎中都笑我，说这才怀身多久，从未听说谁家孩子这个时候便有动静的。可我就是觉得，是咱的孩子机灵，学什么都快呢。

我昨日从院子里摘了一枝带雪的梅，插在瓶里，日日望着，便好似瞧见了往后的好日子。郎君，可否替云娘再拾一枝滹沱河畔的花草？待你归家，我便将它们编在一处，像你与我，作那连理枝，永远也不分开了。

云娘
en:
To my husband, Qian Duo,

It is I, Yunniang. The days have turned colder of late, and snow has begun to gather in the courtyard. I do not know whether it lies thicker or thinner than the snow in the north. Father and Mother take good care of me, yet they speak of you every day, never knowing when you may return.

Life away from home is hard. Now that the weather has turned cold, do remember to add more clothes and eat hot food. Do not neglect yourself. They all say the north is in turmoil, though I do not know how grave it truly is. Only keep this in mind: your master never wished for anyone to avenge him. He only wished that you and your senior brother might both live well. I think the same. When you have the chance, do pass along my regards to Brother Jin Zhong as well.

Not long after you left, I learned that I was with child. Soon, we shall have a child of our own. These past few nights, whenever I sleep, I keep feeling the child stir within me. Even the doctor laughs and says it has only been a short while, and that he has never heard of a child moving so early. Yet I know it must be our child, bright and quick in all things.

Yesterday, I cut a plum branch tipped with snow from the courtyard and set it in a vase. Each time I look at it, I feel as though I can already glimpse the good days to come. My dear husband, would you bring me another flower or sprig of grass from the banks of the Hutuo River? When you return home, I will bind them together, yours and mine, and make of them a pair of joined branches, never to be parted again.

Yunniang
