肩不能扛，手不能提，拉不开弓，跑两步就喘。

既然拿不动刀，那就拿这个吧。
同朝为官的好友文伯把笛子塞进孩子手里，说他看出这孩子通音律，学得快。
韩通不屑一顾：吹拉弹唱，能有啥用？
文伯顿了顿，说：有用。南唐有座“醉花阴”，借着笙歌曼舞，听尽了天下人心。

守谅南下的时候，还在咳个不停。
文伯总夸他笛子吹得好听，乃是天籁。
韩通是个武夫，听不明白好坏，或许也只是因为太忙了，哪有时间停下来好好听曲。
他想，等仗打完了，等天下太平了，就有功夫听这个病恹恹的小子，站在院子里，给他吹一支完整的曲。
到时候就终于可以好好品一品，文伯嘴里这“天大的本事”，到底是个什么动静。
en:
Han Tong had a fiery temper, yet his son turned out to be a hunchback.
He could not carry a load. He could barely lift a thing. He could not draw a bow, and after only a few steps, he was already out of breath.

Since he could not wield a blade, he might as well take this instead.
Wenbo, a close friend and fellow official, pressed a flute into the boy's hand. He said the boy had an ear for music and learned quickly.
Han Tong scoffed. "What use is singing and playing?"
Wenbo paused, then said, "Useful. In Southern Tang, there is a place called Velvet Shade. With song and dance, it has listened to the hearts of all under heaven." 

When Shouliang left for the south, he was still coughing badly.
Wenbo was always praising his flute, saying it sounded like music from heaven.
Han Tong was a soldier and knew nothing about music. Maybe he truly could not hear the difference, or maybe he was simply too busy to stop and listen.
He thought that when the war was over and peace returned, he would finally have time to hear that sickly boy stand in the yard and play a full tune for him.
Then he could finally find out what sort of "great gift" Wenbo had been talking about all along.

少侠亲启：

en:
Young Wanderer,
After leaving Qinghe, I wandered around the area for a couple of days. Just when I was starting to feel bored for lack of anyone to trade blows with, a few roadside thieves came looking for trouble.
Good thing all these years of practice were not for nothing. After a few exchanges, the young fools had lost all stomach for it.
They were strong, able-bodied lads. With strength like that, they could have made an honest living anywhere, yet they chose to block the road and play at being kings of the hill. Still, I could tell they had been driven to it by hard times.
So I pointed a few of them toward Kaifeng to enlist in the army. The others said the capital was too far and wanted to try their hand at small trade instead, so I sent them your way to Qinghe. You should be seeing them before long.
I also picked up some new wine along the way. We will drink it together when we meet.
Good, good. I shall wait.

en:
[Animal I]

[Swallow]

Ode to the Swallow
Zhang Jiuling
The sea swallow is small and slight in size; it comes with spring, a transient guest in the skies.
It knows not that mud is humble and low; it only sees the jade hall's open glow.
Through embroidered doors, it enters two by two; by painted halls, how many times it flew.
I bear no heart for worldly strife or chase; O hawks and falcons, do not guess my place.

Swallowcall
Du Fu
They do not only shun the frost and snow; but how their mates are few, and loneliness does grow.
Through all four seasons they keep their time; in the eighth moon they know to climb.
Will spring's hues ever come to visit me? My young ones still can recognize their destiny.
If the old nest should not be ruined whole, I'll fly again beside my master's soul.

Late Swallow
Bai Juyi
All birds have raised their young, their task is done; the autumn swallow lingers, left alone.
The time to leave the nest is drawing near; why still carry mud with doubtful cheer?
Not knowing that the season is too late; in vain it spends its labor and its fate.
The human world is just the same, I find; not only swallows build their nests in kind.

Swallow
Li Shangyin
No more twittering, the old nest is bare; half-open curtains let the breeze in air.
Where in high towers can we see the pair? For whom do they fly to the painted hall fair?

[Wild Goose]

A Poem on Wild Geese, Written in the South
Wei Chengqing
Southward I go ten thousand miles from home; northward the spring geese fly, and not to roam.
I wonder when the time will come, you see; that I can come back home again with thee.

Lone Goose I
Du Fu
The lonely swan won't drink or eat; its cries recall its kind's defeat.
Who pities this lone shadow, lost in cloud, from all the rest in misty shroud?
It gazes far as if it still could meet; its grief redoubles like a drumbeat fleet.
The crows have no such feeling; they just crowd and clamor loud and proud.

Homebound Goose
Qian Qi
Why from the Xiao and Xiang do you so soon return? The water green, sand bright, with moss on banks, we learn.
When twenty-five strings play at night their plaintive tone, you can't endure and thus you turn.

Early Goose
Du Mu
At Golden River, mid-autumn, bows are bent; and from the clouds, the startled flocks in sorrow sent.
The bronze palm's moonlit shadow passes lone; and from the dim-lit palace, voices come in moan.
You know the Tartar horsemen are in throng; they cannot go back with spring wind, all along.
Do not disdain the Xiaoxiang's lonely place; with wild rice and berries by the water's face.

[Crane]

Two Laments for the Crane I
Liu Yuxi
A lonely pair of cranes in silence stand; their master lives in the Western Capital's land.
Their former nest in Wu's garden trees they know; deep in Luoyang's courtyard, the city's row.
They pace among the bamboos, slow and mild; their hearts embrace the clouds with feelings wild.
Who cares for the fair moon and breeze at night? The neighbor plays the flute with all his might.

Crane
Du Mu
Its pure notes greet the moonlit dawn; it stands in reeds, with thoughts forlorn.
Its red crown like a beauty's cheek; its white plumes like old sages' streak.
The clouds are wild, the egrets coarse; their spirits rough, without remorse.
All day no mate, it stays alone; by the stream it mourns its own.

[Heron]

Quatrain
Du Fu
Two golden orioles sing in willows green, a row of white egrets to the blue sky lean.
My window frames the western snow with sheen, and by the gate a boat from Wu is seen.

The White Egret
Liu Yuxi
The egret white, of noblest grace.
Its plumage rivals snow in white. While other birds make noisy plight, it stands in pensive solitary night.
It sleeps alone on grass so green, and lingers long on stones that gleam.
The front hills have no cloud in sight; it flies into the azure light.

Heron
Du Mu
White feathered with a beak of jade sheen, they fish in the stream's shadowy scene.
Startled, they fly to the green hills' screen, like pear blossoms in the evening serene.
What kind of move was that?

Okay, customers are coming. I'll stop here. 
Stay warm, fed, and safe out there.

zh:
光阴流逝，月轮不知过了多少圆缺。尘世的光阴比村里的跑得更快。
曾经善良的望舒郎，已经变成了慈祥的望舒翁。
他记不得自己走过了多少地方，捞起来多少轮月亮。
但他的歌谣已经成了传说。每一个河西的孩子都会吟唱：月亮光光，快把网张……
人们都说，吃了月光变成的馍馍，就能想起最开心的事。
望舒翁笑笑，不置可否。
也许是安宁的生活让人们忘了一个最朴素的道理：能吃一口饱饭，本就是世上最开心的事。
不过，吟唱童谣的孩子们未曾经过食不果腹的苦难，所以才愿意相信馍馍有令人心悦的玄妙功用。
这样，也挺好，不是么。
en:
Time passed; countless moons waxed and waned. Time in the mortal world runs faster than in the villages. 
The once-kind young Wangshu had become the benevolent old man. 
He couldn't remember how many places he had walked, how many moons he had scooped up. 
But his song had become a legend. Every child in Hexi could sing: Moonlight bright, cast your net right... 
People said that eating a moon-turned-bun would make you remember your happiest memory. 
Old Wangshu would just smile, neither confirming nor denying. 
Perhaps peaceful lives had made people forget the simplest truth: to eat your fill is itself the happiest thing. 
But the children singing the rhyme had never known hunger, so they were willing to believe in the bun's magical power to bring joy. 
And that's fine too, isn't it?
Hum Rice When Unsure

本人的优点罗列如下：

一、我的个子很小，狗洞都能钻过，能帮你发现常人所不能找到的宝贝。
二、我不挑食，路边蘑菇也爱生吃，见过很多新鲜玩意，可以给你提供灵感。

en:
Mother says I am finally old enuff to go to skool, so I need to find one.

It just so happens that Huzi told me he met a Great Elder from Mohist City while helping his grandma pick up firewood. I figure if you are someone Huzi knows, you must be really awsum! So I decided to listen to Mother and write down some of my best points, so you can pick me to be your disciple!

Here is a list of why I am great:

First, I am very small. I can even squeeze through dog holes to help you find treasures that normal people cannot reach.
Second, I am not a picky eater. I even like eating raw mushrooms from the side of the road! I have seen lots of weird stuff, which can give you great ideas.
Third, I have been helping my mother with her experiments since I was little. Even though they blow up a lot, I am the best at cheering people up!

Haha, now that I look at it, I have so many good points! Maybe I do not even need to go to skool after all?
Anyway, Elder Bird, write back fast!

“噗嘶——”
“您说什么？”

"Hnnhg... ah..."
"Heaven hasn't abandoned us after all! Heaven protect the Great Tang!"
"He's dead... He took one with poison..."
"Hsssss..."
"What was that?"
"It's nothing. Come here, child."
"You helped me kill that villain and saved me. Naturally, I will reward you."
"I don't want anything from you. Just let me go. I just want to go to Qingzhou."
"Come closer. Give me the antidote, and let me feel your face."
"Why go to Qingzhou? Come back to the palace with me. Be my daughter. You'll have people waiting on you hand and foot..."
"In Qingzhou... In Qingzhou I'll have..."
"From now on, you'll live a life of riches."

zh: “石敢当”之名最早见于西汉史游所编的儿童启蒙识字书。 唐代学者颜师古对此注解道：“敢当，所向无敌也。”唐代将石敢当与石刻联系，将其视为镇宅辟邪的祥物。至宋时，随着泰山崇拜的盛行，民间为了赋予石敢当更强的神力，将其与作为“五岳之尊”和“幽冥主宰”的泰山信仰相融合，出现了“泰山石敢当”。
en:
The name Shigandang (literally "one who dares resist all") first appeared in a children's literacy primer compiled by Shi You during the Western Han dynasty. Tang dynasty scholar Yan Shigu later explained the phrase as meaning "invincible in the face of all threats." Over time, the concept evolved into physical warding stones inscribed with the name and placed near homes to repel evil spirits.
By the Song dynasty, as Mount Tai worship grew in popularity, people merged these protective markers with beliefs surrounding Mount Tai, revered as the foremost of the Five Sacred Peaks and a ruler of the underworld. In doing so, they endowed it with even greater spiritual power, giving rise to the form known as "Mount Tai Warding Stones" (Taishan Shigandang).

那就是亭长。
没人说得清它什么时候开始住在那儿的，学子们起初只唤它“橘咪”，后来发现它常驻亭中，便封它为一亭之长。
讲堂里夫子讲经，底下坐着一片白衫。亭长有时会蹲在最后一排的蒲团上，耳朵竖着，尾巴收得规规矩矩。夫子偶尔看它一眼，也不赶，只道：“尔亦来闻道乎？”它便轻轻“喵”一声，像是应了。
“它听懂了。”学子们啧啧称奇。
后来大家在亭子里看书，它就蹲在坐垫中间，脑袋凑过来，眼睛跟着字行移动。谁要是念出声来，它就把下巴搁在那人膝上，眯着眼听。念对了，它不动，念错了，爪子就上来了。
有一回一个冒失鬼把“春江水暖鸭先知”念成了“鹅先知”，亭长啪啪连拍三下，拍得那人赶紧翻书去查。
大家都说它肚子里有学问。有人说见过它用爪子在地上划字，像个“之”字。有人说它听夫子讲到《论语》时会打盹，讲到《易经》反倒精神，可见只拣难的听。
这些传说不一而足，但有一点所有人都同意——亭长是一只满腹经纶的博学猫。
月亮升起来的时候，偶尔能听见亭长轻轻地“喵”一声，像在温习白天的功课。
en:
The pavilion held only two cushions: one to the left, and one to the right. The space in between was left open, just enough for a cat to curl up in. That cat was the Pavilion Chief. No one could say quite when it had taken up residence there. The students had at first called it simply "Orange," but when they found it a permanent fixture of the pavilion, they bestowed upon it the title of Chief.
When the master held forth on the classics in the lecture hall before rows of white-robed students, Chief would sometimes take up its place on a cushion in the last row, ears pricked and tail folded with perfect propriety. The master would glance at it now and then but never drove it away, only saying with a smile, "Hast thou also come to hear the Way?" The cat would let out a soft meow, as if in answer. "It understood every word," the students marveled.
Thereafter, when the students gathered in the pavilion to read, Chief would crouch between the cushions, leaning its head in close to follow the lines of characters with its eyes. If anyone read aloud, it would rest its chin upon that person's knee and listen with half-closed eyes. If they read correctly, it sat still; if they erred, a swift paw would come down at once. On one occasion, a careless student misread the verse "the duck is first to know when the spring river grows warm" as "the goose is first to know", and Chief struck three times in rapid succession, sending the student scrambling to check the text.
All agreed it was a cat of considerable learning. Some claimed to have seen it trace a character in the dirt with its claw, something resembling the character "zhi." Others said it would nap when the master lectured on The Analects, yet perk up at the Book of Changes, proving it chose only the most profound passages to attend to.
Such tales were many and varied, yet on one point everyone was in agreement: Chief was a cat of deep erudition. When the moon rose, one could sometimes hear Chief let out a soft, quiet meow, as though reviewing the day's lessons in peace.

zh: 晋王负义，遣铁骑追袭高思继。其帐下一蒙面谋士，暗遣死士携舆图与酒葫而至。高思继饮尽残酿，醉意催发，竟于绝地施展开来，拳走游龙，步踏醉鹤，杀透重围。此后隐姓埋名，立横剑山庄，将此醉中所得拳法并酒葫传于后人，代代相承，未使断绝。
en: Betrayed by the treacherous Prince of Jin, Gao Siji found himself relentlessly hunted by armored cavalry. Yet from the Prince's own camp, a masked advisor secretly dispatched an envoy, bearing a map and a gourd of wine. Downing the fiery brew, Gao Siji let the intoxication take the reins. Cornered against impossible odds, he unleashed his absolute prime, his fists striking like surging dragons, his steps weaving like a drunken crane, and carved a bloody path through the siege. Leaving his true name behind, he vanished into obscurity to found Crossblade Manor. There, he passed down both the legendary gourd and the martial art forged in that desperate hour, ensuring his legacy would endure unbroken through the ages.

zh:
卧佛寺养过许多猫。
有的小猫，合了贵人的眼缘，抱走了，去了富贵之地享福，好过在这儿清修吃苦。善事一桩。
也曾有人想抱走净宗本尊，可它一被揽入怀中，便挣扎着跳出，跳上了大佛头顶，怎么也不肯下来。
师太说：“猫有灵性，其命有九，乃通、灵、静、正、觉、光、精、气、神。”
净宗本尊，是只有灵性的猫呢。
于是它就一直待到现在，待到很多人伸出又缩回手，待到很多小猫来了又走。如今，净宗本尊年岁已高，却是卧佛寺唯一的猫猫。
en:
Many cats have called the Reclining Buddha Temple home. 
Some kittens caught the gaze of kind strangers and were carried away to lives of comfort and ease—far from the temple's quiet austerity. A blessing, no doubt. 
Once, someone tried to take Sacred Master. But whenever it was held, it wriggled free and leapt atop the statue's head, stubbornly refusing to come down. 
The nun said, "Cats carry nine lives, each brimming with essence—intelligence, spirit, tranquility, righteousness, awakening, light, vitality, energy, and soul." 
Sacred Master was no ordinary cat; it was a creature of true spirit. 
So it remained, watching hands reach out then retract, as many little cats came and went. Now old and alone, it is the temple's last guardian.

zh:
游侠，见字如面。
前些时日，老朽随府尹大人巡查蒙学，见学堂里的娃娃们一个个正襟危坐，埋首书卷，连我等走近了都未曾察觉。
老朽心下好奇，是何等妙文，能让这些上蹿下跳的娃娃们如此专心？一问才知，他们手中所读，竟是你前些时日所赠。
老朽又问，这些书好在何处？娃娃们七嘴八舌，老朽这才知道，原来你竟为每个孩子都择了不同的书，实在是费心了。而听闻老朽与你相熟，他们都央着我，定要代他们向你道声谢。
只是，真要问他们想说什么，这群小家伙却面露羞赧，讷讷而止了。最后，老朽想了个法子，让他们把想说的话都诉诸笔端，一并封在信里了。至于写了什么，老朽绝未偷看！
对了，娃娃们还托我转交几幅画作，说是读了书卷后的有感而发。他们都说，游侠你是他们见过最有眼光的人，定能欣赏他们的大作。
哈哈，看来往后若再有与孩子们打交道的差事，找游侠准是没错了。
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/68ce4178e00fee4d12359202E8cIewMG06' size='1174*1638' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>

en:
Dear Wanderer,

The other day, I accompanied the Prefect on an inspection of the village school. The children sat straight at their desks, noses buried in scrolls, so absorbed they didn't even notice us draw near.
Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

en:
[II]

Outside, one receives a tutor's teachings; inside, one upholds a mother's example.
Aunts and uncles should be treated as one's own parents; nephews and nieces as one's own children.
Brothers, bound by deep affection, share the same breath and grow from linked branches.
Friends should share common purpose, encouraging and admonishing one another.
Benevolence and compassion should never be abandoned, even in moments of urgency.
Integrity, righteousness, honesty, and humility should hold firm, even amid hardship and adversity.
A tranquil nature brings ease of spirit; a restless heart brings weariness of soul.
Holding to truth brings fulfillment; chasing worldly things leads the heart astray.
Uphold refined conduct, and honor and rank will naturally follow.
The capitals of China: two great cities, east and west.
Backed by Mount Mang, facing the Luo River; bordered by the Wei, resting upon the Jing.
Palaces coil and rise in grandeur; towers and terraces soar, startling the eye.
They painted birds and beasts, and depicted immortals in splendor.
Side chambers open to the wings; the royal tents face the pillars.
They spread the mats and laid the feast, striking se and blowing sheng.
Ascending the steps to the throne, their caps' pendants glimmered like scattered stars.
To the right lies the Guangnei Hall; to the left, the Chengming Hall.
They gathered ancient classics and canons, and assembled talents of every kind.
Du's drafts, Zhong's clerical script, lacquer writings, and wall-hidden classics.
Generals and ministers filled the courts; nobles and officials lined the roads like locust trees.
Households were granted eight counties; families were provided a thousand soldiers.
Tall-capped officials accompanied the carriages, wheels rolling and tassels swaying.
Generations of nobility grew ever more prosperous, with carriages swift and garments light.
Their merits were recorded and their deeds honored, inscribed on steles and carved in stone.
Yi Yin toiled at Panxi, aiding the age as chief minister.
He ruled over Qufu; who but Duke Dan could have managed it so well?
Duke Huan united the states, aiding the weak and upholding the fallen.
Qi Li restored Emperor Hui of Han; Fu Yue moved King Wuding to virtue.
With able and righteous men laboring diligently, many talents brought peace to the realm.
Jin and Chu took turns as hegemons; Zhao and Wei struggled against the Qin alliance.
They borrowed passage to destroy Guo, and swore oaths at Jiantu.
He Xiao followed the simple laws; Han's excess brought harsh punishments.
Qi, Jian, Lian, and Mu were the finest generals in the art of war.
Their might spread across the desert, their fame echoing through painted portraits.
The Nine Provinces bore Yu's footprints; the Hundred Commanderies were united under Qin.
Mount Tai stands foremost among peaks; there the emperors held their sacrificial rites.
Yanmen and the Purple Frontier, Jitian and Chicheng.
Kunming Lake and Jieshi, Juye Marsh and Dongting Lake.
Vast and boundless stretch the lands, deep and dim lie the mountain caves.
Governance is rooted in agriculture; one must attend diligently to farming.
At the start of spring we till the southern fields; there I plant my millet and grain.
Taxes are paid with the ripe harvest, tribute offered fresh; rewards and demotions follow merit.

zh:
自吐蕃陷凉、甘，隔绝不通。河西、安西、北庭孤悬外域，交兵无援，死伤无算。

大历九年，河西观察判官李秀璋十年连战，率部力战而殁。
建中初，伊州刺史袁光庭督众死守，上下同心。粮尽，自焚以殉。
贞元二年，沙州守将阎朝苦撑十余载，为保百姓，委质吐蕃。遭吐蕃投毒靴中，殁。
贞元五年，西州都督府长史李重晖及部经年固守，及身死，城乃陷。
贞元七年，北庭大都护杨袭古为颉于迦斯诱杀，两千兵甲无还者。
贞元八年，北庭戍卒尽殁，西州全境陷，音信皆绝。安西大都护郭昕、镇守使鲁阳、郑据、杨日佑并四镇戍卒，坚守未退，自此，莫知存亡。

后世论，元和三年，武威郡王、安西四镇节度使郭昕殉节，安西终没。

安史以来，安西、北庭将士四万众困守飞地，历四十余载，大小数百战,存者不过百，皆白发成卒。无归者。

青史寥寥几笔，忠魂一缕千秋。
en:
Since Tubo captured Liangzhou and Ganzhou, communication has been cut off. Hexi, Anxi, and Beiting were left isolated beyond the borders, fighting without reinforcements, suffering countless casualties. 

In the ninth year of Dali, Li Xiuzhang, the Magistrate of Hexi, fought continuously for ten years and died in battle with his troops. 
Early in the Jianzhong era, Yuan Guangting, the Governor of Yizhou, led the defense to the death, with everyone united. When food ran out, he set himself on fire as a martyr. 
In the second year of Zhenyuan, Yan Chao, the defending general of Shazhou, held out for over a decade. To protect the people, he surrendered to Tubo. He was poisoned by Tubo through his boots and died. 
In the fifth year of Zhenyuan, Li Chonghui, the chief clerk of the Xizhou Commander's Office, and his troops defended steadfastly for years. After his death, the city fell. 
In the seventh year of Zhenyuan, Yang Xigu, the Grand Protector of Beiting, was lured and killed by Il ugasi. Two thousand soldiers never returned. 
In the eighth year of Zhenyuan, all Beiting garrison soldiers perished, and the entire Xizhou region fell, cutting off all communication. Guo Xin, the Grand Protector of Anxi, along with garrison commanders Lu Yang, Zheng Ju, Yang Riyou, and the soldiers of the four garrisons, held their ground without retreating. From then on, their fate remained unknown. 

Later historians note that in the third year of Yuanhe, Guo Xin, the Prince of Wuwei and Governor of the Anxi Four Garrisons, died a martyr, and Anxi was finally lost. 

Since the An Lushan Rebellion, the forty thousand soldiers of Anxi and Beiting held out in isolated territories for over forty years, fighting hundreds of battles. Fewer than a hundred survived, all white-haired veterans. None returned. 

A few sparse lines in history, yet their loyal souls endure for millennia.

zh:
福禄寿那三个小娃娃不认字，又想写封信给你，便缠我这老头子代笔，她们说些什么，我便如实写什么，你可莫嫌琐碎。
小福：老山你这样写……大个子，那天熔炉分别之后，我们几个都很担心你。
小寿：不要这么写！我才没有担心那个傻大个子呢。
小福：可是你那时候急得在屋子里转来转去，走得福福眼睛都晕了。
小寿：我才没有呢！笨蛋福福，你记错了！
小禄：别闹啦，我们不是要跟$T(2001)说宝贝的事情吗？老山你这样写，我们担心你，便又潜入熔炉去找你，没曾想你那么厉害，已经杀了出去，我们便捡了些宝贝出来，这些宝贝我们用不上，便一致决定还是交给你。
小寿：我可没说要给$T(30)。
小禄：好好好，你没说，是我和福福说的。
小寿：那也不能只写你们俩……
小福：福福懂了！阿寿这个叫驴唇不对马嘴。
小禄：是口是心非吧？
小寿：福福你说我是驴？！
小福：我我我没有啊……你怎么会觉得你是驴？
……
唉，小福和小寿吵起来了，小禄忙着劝架，吵得老头我脑瓜子嗡嗡的，也不知道要闹到什么时候才完。罢了，不等她们了，游侠你有空了，便来鬼市老头的付坟典店里头取她们从熔炉带出来的宝贝吧。
en:
Those three little rascals—Fu, Lu, and Shou—can't read or write, but they insisted on sending you a letter. So, this old man will be writing it for them. Whatever they said, I wrote, so don't mind the rambling.

Fu: Old Shan, write this: Big Guy, after we parted ways at the Furnace, we were all really worried about you.

Shou: Don't write that! I wasn't worried about that big dumb-dumb at all!

Fu: But you were! You were running in circles so fast, Fu-Fu's eyes got dizzy!

Shou: No, I wasn't! You remembered wrong, dummy Fu-Fu!

Lu: Stop arguing! Weren't we going to tell $T(2001) about the treasure? Old Shan, write this: we were worried, so we snuck back into the Furnace to find you. But turns out you're so strong, you'd already fought your way out! We picked up some treasures along the way. Since these are no use to us, we all agreed they should go to you.

Shou: I never said to give them to $T(30)!

Lu: Fine, fine! You didn't say this, it was me and Fu-Fu.

Shou: Then don't make it sound like just you two decided!

Fu: Oh! I understand! A'Shou's being... um... donkey lips and horse mouth?

Lu: Don't you mean saying one thing but meaning another?

Shou: Little Fu, did you just call me a donkey?!

Fu: I-I-I did not! Why would you think you're a donkey?!

...

Sigh. Now Little Fu and Little Shou are fighting, Little Lu's trying to break it up,
and this old man's head is spinning from the noise. Who knows when they'll stop.

Anyway, I won't wait on them anymore.
Wanderer, when you have time, come by the old man's "Sepulchral Curios" shop in the Ghostlight Market. You can pick up the treasures they brought back from the Buried Tomes.

zh: 观世音菩萨，尊号“大慈大悲救苦救难观世音菩萨”，新译作“观自在”。阿弥陀三尊之一，位左。据《悲华经》记载，阿弥陀佛过去生中为转轮王无诤念时，长子不眴于宝藏如来处发愿称，若有众生遭受苦恼恐怖等事，能够忆念、称念其名号，即为其免除如此种种痛苦烦恼，宝藏佛即为其授记，命名“观世音”。
en:
Known by the honorific title "Greatly Compassionate and Merciful Guanyin, Savior from Suffering and Peril", Guanyin is also called Avalokitesvara, "the One Who Perceives the Sounds of the World."
One of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Pure Land, she stands to the left of Amitabha Buddha. According to the Sutra of the Flower of Compassion, in a past life Amitabha was the Wheel-Turning King Wuzhengnian, whose eldest son Bu Xun made a vow before the Buddha. He swore: "If any sentient being faces fear, suffering, or calamity, and calls my name with focused mind, I shall deliver them from pain and distress." Thus the Buddha gave him the name Guanyin.

祖父常言，万物有声。在其研制留声匣的岁月里，不知鼓捣出多少声响，竹简开合的脆响、纸墨相触的窣窣、机枢转动的沉吟。可墨道总不受其扰，任这万般声音流过，依旧睡得酣沉。祖父也曾蹑手蹑脚地捧着留声匣贴近它毛茸茸的脸颊，存下它一起一伏的呼噜声——时而细若幼子的鼻息呼呼，时而绵如灶上暖水咕嘟。
祖父觉得有趣，偶尔也对它发问：“墨道墨道，你这般能睡，可是在梦里听见了我听不见的妙音？”
墨道只将身子蜷得更圆些，仿佛这世间纷繁声响，都不过是它梦的陪衬。
祖父不禁想起了捡回墨道的那一日，墙头传来细弱喵鸣，竟与匣中自己刚录的暴雨声一高一低，自成曲调。
他这一生，或终难寻得墨道之声为何。但这只小猫，与自己有缘。
偶有一次，墨道忽从梦中醒转。
那时祖父正独自一人排练着当年的墨道训格，墨道轻轻走过去，用脑袋蹭了蹭祖父的手背，喵叫一声，恰好被转动的留声匣永远留了下来。据余歌所说，这就是祖父生前最后一次合唱。
后来，祖父不在了。
墨道依然能一觉睡到日头西斜。
这屋里再也没了昔日的吵闹动静，按理说无人叨扰，梦，应该更安稳了。
可如今墨道每次在这醒来，总觉得这满屋子的寂静，好像比从前所有声音加起来，都更令它心头喧嚣。
它舔舔爪子，朝天喵叫一声。
这一声，不由自主地比以往都更响些——
似在等某人应和。
en:
If you wish to know what the Mohist Voice is, you should first ask Mohway. Yes, that black furball usually curled up asleep at Yu Ge's grandfather's desk.
Grandfather often said that all things have a sound. During the years he spent developing the voice box, he created countless noises: the crisp snap of bamboo slips, the rustle of paper meeting ink, the low hum of turning gears. Yet Mohway was never disturbed, sleeping soundly through every sound. Grandfather would tiptoe to the cat, holding the voice box near its furry cheek to capture its rising and falling purrs. Sometimes as faint as a child's breath, sometimes as steady as water simmering on a stove.
Grandfather found it amusing and would occasionally ask, "Mohway, Mohway, you sleep so much; have you heard a wonderful sound in your dreams that I cannot?"
Mohway would only curl into a tighter circle, as if all the world's complex noises were merely background for its dreams.
Grandfather couldn't help but remember the day he found Mohway. A faint meow from the wall harmonized perfectly with the rain he had just recorded, forming a melody of its own.
In this life, he might never discover what the true "Mohist Voice" was. But this kitten and he were meant to be.
Once, Mohway suddenly woke from a dream.
Grandfather was practicing his old training verses alone. Mohway walked over softly, nuzzled Grandfather's hand, and let out a meow that was captured forever by the spinning voice box. According to Yu Ge, that was Grandfather's final duet.
Later, Grandfather was gone.
Mohway still sleeps until the sun dips low.
The house no longer holds the old bustle. Logically, with no one to disturb it, the dreams should be more peaceful.
But now, every time Mohway wakes here, the silence of the room feels louder than all the previous sounds combined.
It licks its paws and lets out a meow to the sky.
This cry is louder than usual, as if by instinct.
As if waiting for someone to answer.

《清异录》载，孙承佑宴客时指其盘筵曰：“今日座中，南之蝤蛑（青蟹），北之红羊，东之虾鱼，西之粟米，无不毕备，可谓富小四海矣。”
然蟹有岁时之限，巧匠遂思以鱼代蟹，取蟹膏蟹黄之精华，融于秘制芡汁，令鱼肉入口即迸极鲜蟹味。
en:
The people of Hangzhou love crab. In the early Song dynasty, when Qian Kun sought a post outside the capital, someone asked which prefecture he desired. He replied, "Any place with crab and no vice prefect will do." People told it as a joke for years, but it does say something about the allure of fresh crab.
Records of Strange Things recounts how Sun Chengyou gestured to the dishes at his banquet and declared: "At this table today, we have the mud crabs of the south, red mutton of the north, shrimp and fish of the east, and millet of the west. Nothing is lacking. One might well call this wealth from all four corners of the earth."
Yet crab has its season, so a clever cook turned to fish, blending the essence of crab roe and fat into a secret sauce that makes the fish burst with crab flavor at first bite.

zh:
朝笏，又称笏板或手板，为君臣朝会时所执礼器。不同品阶官员上朝时所持朝笏不同：三品以上玉笏，五品象笏。品阶更低的官员则执竹木笏。
朝笏虽材质迥异，但尺寸统一，皆为一尺二寸长，上窄下宽。其上可记官员意欲参奏之事，或是官家旨意。此外，借以笏板之型，官员可于朝会时遮蔽口秽，以示对官家的尊敬。
en:
The court tablet, also known as a hu tablet, was a ceremonial baton held by officials during audiences. Its material reflected rank: third rank and above used jade, fifth rank used ivory, and lower ranks used bamboo or wood. Materials varied, but the size was standardized at one chi and two cun, narrow at the top and wider at the base.
Officials could jot down matters they wished to present, or record the emperor's instructions. It could also be raised to cover the mouth during an audience, a small gesture of propriety and respect.

Though I have followed you faithfully these years, I am all too aware of my own limitations—modest talents that fall far short of greatness.
After the Inkbound Order incident, I believed your heart had turned away from worldly affairs. So I retreated alongside you, dedicating myself quietly to martial practice and seeking solace in the landscape.
Yet I never expected your determination would burn so fiercely. I thought we came here just to master a decisive technique to defeat our foes—how naïve I was.
You are a soaring eagle, while I, a humble sparrow. So, how could I grasp your lofty ambitions?
I do not wish to hinder your path. With that, I take my leave.
The way stretches endlessly ahead. Who knows when we'll meet again? Take care.

zh: 碧霞元君，全称"东岳泰山天仙玉女碧霞元君"，道教尊奉之泰山山神，主司庇佑众生、统摄岳府神兵、照察人间善恶。汉魏时，泰山女神传说初现，张华《博物志》等载有泰山神女故事，曹操诗中“仙人玉女”为其雏形。三国至唐，玉女形象借曹植、李白诗作传播，与泰山关联加深，宋代确认“碧霞元君”之名。
en:
Lady Bixia, whose full title translates to the "Heavenly Immortal Lady Bixia of the Eastern Peak of Mount Tai," is the revered Daoist goddess of Mount Tai. She watches over the mortal realm, weighing good against evil, protecting the people, and commanding the mountain's heavenly armies.
Legends of a goddess on Mount Tai first appeared during the Han and Wei dynasties, as recorded in Zhang Hua's Compendium. The "immortal jade maiden" mentioned in Cao Cao's poetry is considered her earliest prototype. Her legend grew throughout the Three Kingdoms and Tang dynasty periods, popularized by renowned poets like Cao Zhi and Li Bai. By the Song dynasty, she was officially bestowed the title "Lady Bixia."

声声曾经见过人们在庆典时围在高高的大鼓旁边。鼓槌往下一敲，人们就会往鼓前涌去，爆发出阵阵声浪。
后来，声声一次又一次地从高处跳下，用爪子打大鼓。鼓声穿透了凉州的层层大雪，惊吓了山间站得高高的鸟儿，却再也没有一个人因为鼓声围过来。
声声最后一次敲响大鼓，鼓皮破了。它落进鼓里，全身都好疼好疼。
分不清在梦里还是现实，有一双柔软的手把声声捧出来放在心口。声声听到了心脏鼓动的声音，和它敲响大鼓的声音一模一样。
en:
Sound once witnessed crowds gathering around a towering drum during festivals. Each time the mallet struck, waves of cheers surged forward with the sound. 
Time after time, Sound leapt from above, striking the drum with its paws. The deep booms pierced through the heavy snow blanketing Liangzhou. Yet not once did a single soul come rushing to the drum. 
The final strike cracked the drumhead. Sound tumbled inside, aching all over. 
Between dream and waking, gentle hands lifted Sound and held it close to a warm heart. It heard a steady heartbeat—the same deep rhythm as the drum it once played.

水远山长双属玉，身闲心苦一舂锄。
宋时名属玉，其形似巨鸭，长颈修昂，赤目如丹，振翅于惊涛之间，栖息于菰蒲之侧。本为珍禽，至唐宋，属玉自天子之苑飞入江南水乡。盖因其常作夜鸣，似有孤高之感，时人以为江湖逸客。
en:
Far water, long hills, and a pair of herons; idle body, weary heart, like an egret alone.
Known in the Song dynasty as the jade heron, it resembles a great duck, with a long neck held high and eyes as red as cinnabar. It beats its wings amid thunderous waves, and roosts beside the reeds and cattails. Once a rare bird of the emperor's own gardens, by the Tang and Song dynasties, the jade heron had flown into the water-towns of Jiangnan. As it often calls in the night, seeming to carry a solitary, lofty air, people of the time took it for a wandering recluse of the jianghu.
